We again adopt the convention of omitting the subscripts \( a, b \) of \( {\ell }_{a, b},{D}_{a, b} \) , and \( {X}_{a, b} \) .

(i) By Lemma 11.26, in order to show that \( \ell \left( \mathfrak{C}\right) \) is preserved by the ODE, we need to show that for any \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial \mathfrak{C} \) the vector

\[
X\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\ell }^{-1}\left( {\ell {\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }^{2} + \ell {\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }^{\# }}\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } + D\left( \mathbf{R}\right)
\]

is contained in the tangent cone of \( \mathfrak{C} \) . Since, by Proposition 11.42, \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) lies inside the tangent cone of \( \mathfrak{C} \) , it suffices to show that \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) also lies inside the tangent cone of \( \mathfrak{C} \) . However this is true for the following reasons. It follows from Lemma 11.40(ii) that \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the cone of geometrically nonnegative operators. \( {}^{23} \) By Exercise 11.43, \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is contained in the tangent cone of \( \mathfrak{C} \) .

(ii) First observe that \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) being transverse to the boundary of \( \ell \left( \mathfrak{C}\right) \) is equivalent to

\[
X\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } + D\left( \mathbf{R}\right)
\]

being transverse to \( \partial \mathfrak{C} \) . We have \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) is contained in the tangent cone of \( \mathfrak{C} \) . Thus, to show that \( X\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is transverse to \( \partial \mathfrak{C} \) , it suffices to show that \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is a positive curvature operator.

Recall that by (11.66),

\[
D\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {2a}\operatorname{Rc} \land  \operatorname{Rc} + 2{b}^{2}{\operatorname{Rc}}_{0}^{2} \land  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

\[
+ \frac{\sigma {b}^{2}}{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\left( {-n\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} - {4b} + 2}\right) \mathbf{I},
\]

where \( \sigma  = \frac{1}{n}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\operatorname{Rc}}_{0}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \end{Vmatrix}}^{2} \cdot  {}^{24} \) We first assume that \( 0 < b < \bar{b} \) so that

\[
- n\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} - {4b} + 2 > 0.
\]

Case 1. \( \sigma  > 0 \) . Then \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is a positive curvature operator since \( {2a}\operatorname{Rc} \land  \operatorname{Rc} \) and \( 2{b}^{2}{\operatorname{Rc}}_{0}^{2} \land \) id are nonnegative and the coefficient in front of \( \mathbf{I} \) is positive. This implies \( X\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is transverse to \( \partial \mathfrak{C} \) .

Case 2. \( \sigma  = 0 \) . Then \( {\operatorname{Rc}}_{0} = 0 \) , so that \( \operatorname{Rc} = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Scal} \cdot  \mathrm{{id}} > 0 \) since \( \mathbf{R} \neq  0 \) implies Scal \( > 0 \) . Hence

\[
D\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {2a}\operatorname{Rc} \land  \operatorname{Rc} = \frac{2a}{{n}^{2}}{\left( \operatorname{Scal}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \land  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

is a positive curvature operator.

Hence \( X\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is transverse to \( \partial \mathfrak{C} \) when \( b < \bar{b} \) .

---

\( {}^{23} \) Hence \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the cone of nonnegative curvature operators.

\( {}^{24} \) Note that \( D\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is geometrically nonnegative.

---

Now we consider the case where \( b = \bar{b} \) . In this case, by part (iii) of the present proposition (whose proof is independent of part (ii)), we have \( {\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is a positive curvature operator since \( \mathbf{R} \neq  0 \) . This implies

\[
{X}_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}^{-1}\left( {{\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }^{2} + {\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }^{\# }}\right)
\]

is a positive curvature operator and hence transverse to \( \partial \mathfrak{C} \) .

(iii) Finally we show that \( {\ell }_{a, b}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is a positive algebraic curvature operator when \( \mathbf{R} ≢ 0 \) and \( b \) takes the end value \( \bar{b} \) . We divide the proof of this statement into two cases. Let \( {\mu }_{1} \) be the smallest eigenvalue of \( \mathbf{R} \) . Recall

\[
{\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \mathbf{R} + 2\left( {a - \bar{b}}\right) \bar{\lambda }\mathbf{I} + 2\bar{b}\operatorname{Rc} \land  \mathrm{{id}}.
\]

\[
{\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  > 0
\]

since \( a > \bar{b},\bar{b} > 0 \) , and \( \operatorname{Rc} \land \) id is nonnegative.

From formula (11.92) we have \( \mathrm{{Rc}} \geq \; \left( {n - 3}\right) \left| {\mu }_{1}\right| \) . \[
{\mu }_{1}\left( {{\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right)  > {\mu }_{1} + 2\left( {a - \bar{b}}\right) \bar{\lambda } + 2\bar{b}\left( {n - 3}\right) \left| {\mu }_{1}\right|
\]

\[
\geq  {\mu }_{1} + 2\bar{b}\left| {\mu }_{1}\right|  + 2\left( {a - \bar{b}}\right) \bar{\lambda }
\]

\[
= \left( {2\bar{b} - 1}\right) \left| {\mu }_{1}\right|  + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\bar{b}}^{2}\frac{2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n},
\]

where here we have used that \( n \geq  4 \) and \( \bar{\lambda } = \frac{\operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n} = \frac{2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n} \) . By elementary computations we have \( \bar{b} < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{n\left( {n - 2}\right) }} \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) . We may further estimate using (11.91) that

\[
{\mu }_{1}\left( {{\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right)  >  - \left( {1 - 2\bar{b}}\right) \frac{2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\bar{b}}^{2}\frac{2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n}
\]

\[
= \left( {\frac{2}{{n}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4}}\right) \left( {1 - 2\bar{b}}\right) 2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)
\]

since \( {\left( n\left( n - 2\right) \bar{b} + 2\right) }^{2} = {2n}\left( {n - 2}\right)  + 4 \) , so that \( 2\left( {1 - 2\bar{b}}\right)  = n\left( {n - 2}\right) {\bar{b}}^{2} \) . That \( {\ell }_{a,\bar{b}}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is a positive algebraic curvature operator now follows from the fact that \( \frac{2}{{n}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4} \geq  0 \) if \( n \geq  4 \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
We say that an algebraic curvature operator \( \mathbf{R} \) is a nonnegative curvature operator of rank 1 if \( \mathbf{R} = \omega  \otimes  \omega \) for some \( \omega  \in  {\Lambda }^{2}{\mathbb{E}}^{n} \) . An algebraic curvature operator is called geometrically nonnegative if it can be written as the linear combination, with positive coefficients, of nonnegative curvature operators of rank 1.

If \( \mathbf{R} \) is geometrically nonnegative, then \( \mathbf{R} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{c}_{\alpha }{\eta }_{\alpha } \otimes  {\eta }_{\alpha } \) , where \( {c}_{\alpha } > 0 \) . Thus, for any 2-form \( \xi \) we have

\[
\mathbf{R}\left( {\xi ,\xi }\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{c}_{\alpha }{\left( {\eta }_{\alpha }\left( \xi \right) \right) }^{2} \geq  0,
\]

so that \( \mathbf{R} \) is a nonnegative curvature operator.

Note that if \( \omega  \otimes  \omega \) is an algebraic curvature operator, then the first Bianchi identity implies \( \omega  \land  \omega  = 0 \) and hence there exist \( v, w \in  {\mathbb{E}}^{n} \) such that \( {}^{19} \)

\[
\omega  = v \land  w
\]

---

\( {}^{19} \) Indeed, the first Bianchi identity applied to \( \omega  \land  \omega \) implies

\[
{\left( \omega  \land  \omega \right) }_{{ijk}\ell } = \frac{1}{3}\left( {{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }_{k\ell } + {\omega }_{ki}{\omega }_{j\ell } + {\omega }_{jk}{\omega }_{i\ell }}\right)  = 0.
\]

We may prove, by induction on \( n \) , that \( \omega  \land  \omega  = 0 \) implies there exist \( v, w \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) such that \( \omega  = v \land  w \) . The result is clearly true for \( n = 1,2 \) . Now suppose the result is true for dimension \( n - 1 \) , where \( n \geq  4 \) . Let \( {\left\{  {e}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{n} \) be a basis for \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . We may write

\[
\omega  = {e}_{1} \land  x + \eta
\]

where \( x = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \geq  2}}{x}^{i}{e}_{i} \) and \( \eta  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j \geq  2}}{\eta }^{ij}{e}_{i} \land  {e}_{j} \) . From \( \omega  \land  \omega  = 0 \) we find that

\[
{e}_{1} \land  x \land  \eta  = 0\;\text{ and }\;\eta  \land  \eta  = 0.
\]

By our induction assumption, \( \eta  = y \land  z \) , where \( y = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i > 2}}{y}^{i}{e}_{i} \) and \( z = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i > 2}}{z}^{i}{e}_{i} \) . Now since \( n \geq  3,{e}_{1} \land  x \land  \eta  = 0 \) implies \( x \land  y \land  z = 0 \) , so that the vectors \( x, y, z \) are linearly dependent. Without loss of generality, we may assume that \( x = {c}_{1}y + {c}_{2}z \) for some

---

Note also that the Riemann curvature operator of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{n - 2} \) is a nonnegative curvature operator of rank 1.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
We may define the Ricci tensor \( \operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \in  {S}^{2}\left( {\mathbb{E}}^{n}\right) \) corresponding to an algebraic curvature operator \( \mathbf{R} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {{\Lambda }^{2}{\mathbb{E}}^{n}}\right) {\text{ by }}^{15} \)

(11.38)

\[
\left\langle  {\operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \left( {e}_{i}\right) ,{e}_{j}}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left\langle  {\mathbf{R}\left( {{e}_{i} \land  {e}_{k}}\right) ,{e}_{j} \land  {e}_{k}}\right\rangle   = {\mathbf{R}}_{ikjk}.
\]

That is, the Ricci tensor corresponding to an algebraic curvature operator is the same trace as is used to obtain the usual Ricci tensor from the Riemann curvature operator:

\[
\left\langle  {\operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right) \left( {e}_{i}\right) ,{e}_{j}}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left\langle  {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{e}_{i} \land  {e}_{k}}\right) ,{e}_{j} \land  {e}_{k}}\right\rangle   = 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{k},{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 2{R}_{ij}.
\]

CAVEAT. Note that for a Riemannian metric the Ricci tensor of its curvature operator \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) is twice the Ricci curvature tensor of the metric.

We define the scalar curvature associated to an algebraic curvature operator \( \mathbf{R} \) by \( {}^{16} \)

(11.39)

\[
\operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \Doteq  \operatorname{tr}\left( {\operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}_{ikik}.
\]

Hence, for a Riemannian metric, the scalar curvature of the curvature operator, i.e., Scal(Rm), is equal to twice the scalar curvature of the metric.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .

The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

Proof of Theorem 5.2.3. In views of Theorem 5.2.1 and Theorem 5.2.2, we may assume the Ricci curvature (in dimension 3) and the curvature operator (in dimension 4) always have nontrivial kernels somewhere along the Ricci flow.

(i) In the case of dimension 3, we consider the evolution equation (1.3.5) of the Ricci curvature

\[
\frac{\partial {R}_{ab}}{\partial t} = \bigtriangleup {R}_{ab} + 2{R}_{acbd}{R}_{cd}
\]

in an orthonormal frame coordinate. At each point, we diagonalize \( {R}_{ab} \) with eigenvectors \( {e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3} \) and eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{2} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} \) . Since

\[
{R}_{1c1d}{R}_{cd} = {R}_{1212}{R}_{22} + {R}_{1313}{R}_{33}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {{\left( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}\left( {{\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) }\right) ,
\]

we know that if \( {R}_{ab} \geq  0 \) , then \( {R}_{acbd}{R}_{cd} \geq  0 \) . By Hamilton’s strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1), there exists an interval \( 0 < t < \delta \) on which the rank of \( {R}_{ab} \) is constant and the null space of \( {R}_{ab} \) is invariant under parallel translation and invariant in time and also lies in the null space of \( {R}_{acbd}{R}_{cd} \) . If the null space of \( {R}_{ab} \) has rank one, then \( {\lambda }_{1} = 0 \) and \( {\lambda }_{2} = {\lambda }_{3} > 0 \) . In this case, by De Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( M \) of the compact \( M \) splits isometrically as \( \mathbb{R} \times  {\sum }^{2} \) and the curvature of \( {\sum }^{2} \) has a positive lower bound. Hence \( {\sum }^{2} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . Assume \( M = \mathbb{R} \times  {\sum }^{2}/\Gamma \) , for some isometric subgroup \( \Gamma \) of \( \mathbb{R} \times  {\sum }^{2} \) . Note that \( \Gamma \) remains to be an isometric subgroup of \( \mathbb{R} \times  {\sum }^{2} \) during the Ricci flow by the uniqueness (Theorem 1.2.4). Since the Ricci flow on \( \mathbb{R} \times  {\sum }^{2}/\Gamma \) converges to the standard metric by Theorem 5.1.11, \( \Gamma \) must be an isometric subgroup of \( \mathbb{R} \times  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the standard metric. If the null space of \( {R}_{ab} \) has rank greater than one, then \( {R}_{ab} = 0 \) and the manifold is flat. This proves Theorem 5.2.3 part (i).

(ii) In the case of dimension 4, we classify the manifolds according to the (restricted) holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) . Note that the curvature operator has nontrivial kernel and \( \mathcal{G} \) is the image of the the curvature operator, we see that \( \mathcal{G} \) is a proper subalgebra of \( {so}\left( 4\right) \) . We divide the argument into two cases.

Case 1. \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible.

In this case the universal cover \( \widetilde{M} \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) . By the above results on two and three dimensional Ricci flow, we see that \( M \) is diffeomorphic to a quotient of one of the spaces \( {\mathbb{R}}^{4},\mathbb{R} \times  {\mathbb{S}}^{3},{\mathbb{R}}^{2} \times  {\mathbb{S}}^{2},{\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) by a group of fixed point free isometries. As before by running the Ricci flow until it converges and using the uniqueness (Theorem 1.2.4), we see that this group is actually a subgroup of the isometries in the standard metrics.

Case 2. \( \mathcal{G} \) is not reducible (i.e., irreducible).

If the manifold is not Einstein, then by Berger's classification theorem for holonomy groups [7], \( \mathcal{G} = {so}\left( 4\right) \) or \( u\left( 2\right) \) . Since the curvature operator is not strictly positive, \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( 2\right) \) , and the universal cover \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) is Kähler and has positive bisectional curvature. In this case \( \widetilde{M} \) is biholomorphic to \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{2} \) by the result of Andreotti-Frankel [47] (also the resolution of the Frankel conjecture by Mori [96] and Siu-Yau [120]).

If the manifold is Einstein, then by the block decomposition of the curvature operator matrix in four-manifolds (see the third section of Chapter 1),

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\Lambda }_{ + }^{2},{\Lambda }_{ - }^{2}}\right)  = 0.
\]

Let \( \varphi  \neq  0 \) , and

\[
\varphi  = {\varphi }_{ + } + {\varphi }_{ - } \in  {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \oplus  {\Lambda }_{ - }^{2},
\]

lies in the kernel of the curvature operator, then

\[
0 = {Rm}\left( {{\varphi }_{ + },{\varphi }_{ + }}\right)  + {Rm}\left( {{\varphi }_{ - },{\varphi }_{ - }}\right) .
\]

It follows that

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\varphi }_{ + },{\varphi }_{ + }}\right)  = 0\text{ , and }\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\varphi }_{ - },{\varphi }_{ - }}\right)  = 0\text{ . }
\]

We may assume \( {\varphi }_{ + } \neq  0 \) (the argument for the other case is similar). We consider the restriction of \( {Rm} \) to \( {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) , since \( {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) is an invariant subspace of \( {Rm} \) and the intersection of \( {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) with the null space of \( {Rm} \) is nontrivial. By considering the null space of \( {Rm} \) and its orthogonal complement in \( {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) , we obtain a parallel distribution of rank one in \( {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) . This parallel distribution gives a parallel translation invariant two-form \( \omega  \in  {\Lambda }_{ + }^{2} \) on the universal cover \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) . This two-form is nondegenerate, so it induces a Kähler structure of \( \widetilde{M} \) . Since the Kähler metric is parallel with respect to the original metric and the manifold is irreducible, the Kähler metric is proportional to the original metric. Hence the manifold \( \widetilde{M} \) is Kähler-Einstein with nonnegative curvature operator. Taking into account the irreducibility of \( \mathcal{G} \) , it follows that \( \widetilde{M} \) is biholomorphic to \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{2} \) . Therefore the proof of Theorem 5.2.3 is completed. D

(Existence of a generalized pinching set). Let

\[
{C}_{\clubsuit }{\left( s\right) }_{s \in  \lbrack 0,1)} \subset  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right)
\]

be a continuous family of closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant cones of maximum dimension, such that \( {C}_{4}\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) is contained in the half-space of curvature operators with positive scalar curvature for all \( s \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Suppose that for \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) the vector field \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) for all \( s \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Then for any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and \( {h}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) there exists a closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset \( F \subset \; {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) with the following properties:

(1) \( F \) is preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) ;

(2) \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \subset  F \subset  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) ;

(3) \( \overline{F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) } \) is compact (i.e., bounded) for all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) .

Fix any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and \( {h}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) . Define the set \( F \) to be the intersection of all closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subsets of \( {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) satisfying properties (1) and (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.64. We want to show that \( F \) is the desired generalized pinching set. Since \( {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) is such a set, \( F \) is a well-defined closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset contained in \( {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) .

(I) Suppose \( {\mathbf{R}}_{0} \in  F \) and \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) with \( \mathbf{R}\left( 0\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}_{0} \) . Then for any closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset \( G \) of \( {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) satisfying properties (1) and (2), \( {}^{29} \) we have \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right)  \in  G \) . Hence, by definition, \( \mathbf{R}\left( t\right)  \in  F \) . Thus property (1) holds for \( F \) .

(II) It is also clear that property (2) holds for \( F \) , i.e.,

\[
{C}_{\text{ ♣ }}\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \subset  F.
\]

(III) It remains to prove property (3). Suppose, with the goal of obtaining a contradiction, that property (3) is false for \( F \) for some \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) . Let \( {s}_{0} \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) be the infimum of all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) for which property (3) is false for \( F \) , i.e.,

\[
{s}_{0} \Doteq  \inf \{ s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) : F \smallsetminus  {C}_{ \clubsuit  }\left( s\right) \text{ is unbounded }\} .
\]

Then there exists a sequence \( {\left\{  {s}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  \mathbb{N}} \) with \( {s}_{i} \rightarrow  {s}_{0} \) such that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( {s}_{i}\right) \) is unbounded for all \( i \) . We shall obtain the contradiction from showing that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{4}\left( s\right) \) is bounded for any \( s \) sufficiently close to \( {s}_{0} \) .

For \( s \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) define

\[
{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  \Doteq  \text{ the cone over the set }
\]

\[
\left\{  {\mathbf{R} \in  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = 1,\operatorname{dist}\left( {\mathbf{R},\partial {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) }\right)  \geq  \delta }\right\}  ,
\]

which is a slightly smaller cone contained in \( {C}_{4}\left( s\right) \) (with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\delta  \rightarrow  0}}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  = \; \left. {{C}_{4}\left( s\right) }\right) \) . For \( \delta , h > 0 \) define

\[
{T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  \Doteq  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) ,\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  h}\right\}  ,
\]

which is, as noted in [43], a 'truncated shifted cone'. We leave it to the reader to show that both \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) and \( {T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) are closed, convex, and \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant (convexity is the main issue). \( {}^{30} \)

(1) When \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, the cones \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) are preserved by the ODE. For any \( s \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) there exists \( {\delta }_{0} = {\delta }_{0}\left( s\right)  > 0 \) such that for all \( \delta  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  - \{ 0\} \) the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) .

This fact follows from

(i) \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\delta  \rightarrow  0}}\partial {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right)  = \partial {C}_{\Phi }\left( s\right) \) ,

(ii) the continuity of \( Q \) ,

(iii) our assumption that for \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} , Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of tangent cone of \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) , and

(iv) the fact that \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is homogeneous of degree 2, i.e., \( Q\left( {c\mathbf{R}}\right)  = \; {c}^{2}Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) for all \( c \geq  0 \) (which addresses the issue of the noncompactness of the cones).

---

\( {}^{29} \) Note that we do not use property (2) here.

\( {}^{30} \) Note that the set \( \sum  \doteq  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} \in  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = 1}\right\} \) is convex. To prove the convexity of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) , one just needs to show that

\[
\{ \mathbf{R} \in  \sum  : \operatorname{dist}\left( {\mathbf{R},\partial \sum }\right)  \geq  \delta \}
\]

is convex. The convexity of \( {T}_{h}{C}_{\delta }\left( s\right) \) also follows easily.

---

(2) Truncated shifted cones are preserved by the ODE. There exists \( \bar{h} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) (in particular, for \( \bar{h} \) sufficiently large) such that the set

\[
{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  = \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  \bar{h}\}
\]

is preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) for all \( \delta  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }_{0}\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\rbrack \) .

First note that

\[
\partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \subset  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cup  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} .
\]

We have

\[
\operatorname{trace}Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\left| \operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \right| }^{2} \geq  \frac{4}{n}{\left( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \right) }^{2} \geq  \frac{4}{n}{\bar{h}}^{2} > 0
\]

for \( \mathbf{R} \in  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) (note that \( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\left( {\operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right) \) ).

Case (a). Hence for \( \mathbf{R} \) with \( \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h} \) the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  \bar{h}\} \) . This implies that for

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \smallsetminus  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \subset  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} ,
\]

the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) , which is the half-space \( \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  0\} \) .

Case (b). Now assume

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}
\]

\[
\subset  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}
\]

so that in particular trace \( \left( \mathbf{R}\right)  > \bar{h} \) . In this case the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) is the same as the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \) (after shifting the vertex by \( \mathbf{I} \) ).

Let \( {\eta }_{0} \) be the infimum of the distance from \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) among \( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime } \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) with \( \operatorname{trace}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right)  = 1 \) . Since by part (1), \( {\eta }_{0} > 0 \) , we have that the distance from \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) grows quadratically; in particular, it is at least

(11.128)

\[
{\eta }_{0}{\left( \operatorname{trace}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right) \right) }^{2} \geq  c{\eta }_{0}{\left| {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}
\]

for all \( {\mathbf{R}}^{\prime } \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) , where \( c > 0 \) . For \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in \; \left. {\partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\} \)

(i) let \( {d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) be the distance of \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) and

(ii) let \( {d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) be the distance of \( Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right) \) to the boundary of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \) , so that by (11.128)

\[
{d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}\right| }^{2} \geq  \frac{1}{2}c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R}\right| }^{2}
\]

(with the last inequality holding for \( \bar{h} \) large enough). Next observe that

\[
\left| {Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right)  - Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }\right|  = \left| {2\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{R}\# \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{I}\# \mathbf{I}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {A}_{1}\left| \mathbf{R}\right|
\]

for some constant \( {A}_{1} < \infty \) . Hence, by the triangle inequality and the above estimates,

\[
{d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \geq  {d}_{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  - \left| {Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  - Q\left( {\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I}}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2}c{\eta }_{0}{\left| \mathbf{R}\right| }^{2} - {A}_{1}\left| \mathbf{R}\right|
\]

so that \( {d}_{1}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  > 0 \) provided that \( \left| \mathbf{R}\right| \) is sufficiently large. Thus \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) .

Case (c). Finally, if

\[
\mathbf{R} \in  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{I} \in  \partial {C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right\}   \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

then by the arguments in proving Cases (a) and (b), it follows that \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) .

By Cases (a),(b), and (c), we have shown that for all \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial \left( {{T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , the vector \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) .

(3) Given any \( \bar{h} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , there exists \( \delta  > 0 \) (in particular, for \( \delta \) sufficiently small) such that the set \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) is contained in the interior of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) as subsets of the hyperplane \( \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}}\right\} \) . This is geometrically clear from considering the limit as \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) .

(4) By part (3), for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and for \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) , \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} \) is contained in the interior of \( {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \; \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\} \) . We claim that by the definition of \( {s}_{0} \) , for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small there exists \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) (except when \( {s}_{0} = \varepsilon \) , where we let \( \bar{s} = {s}_{0} \) ) and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough such that

(11.129)

\( F \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = k\bar{h}\}  \subset  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \bar{s}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = k\bar{h}\}  \subset  k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) , \) that is,

\[
\frac{1}{k}F \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( \bar{s}\right)  \cap  \{ \mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \bar{h}\}  \subset  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) .
\]

(a) If \( {s}_{0} = \varepsilon  = \bar{s} \) , then the claim is clear since \( F \subset  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) .

(b) If \( {s}_{0} > \varepsilon \) , then \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\Phi }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) is compact for all \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) . Therefore, for each \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {\varepsilon ,{s}_{0}}\right) \) , there exists \( {k}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) such that the first inclusion in (11.129) holds for all \( k \geq  {k}_{0} \) .

(5) By part (4), for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough, the set

\[
{F}^{\prime } \Doteq  \left( {F \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  k\bar{h}}\right\}  }\right)  \cup  \left( {F \cap  k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right) }\right)
\]

is closed, convex, \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant, and preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) . In particular, the convexity of \( {F}^{\prime } \) follows from the inclusion (11.129). Now clearly \( {F}^{\prime } \subset  F \) . On the other hand, by the definition of \( F \) (in particular, its minimality), we have \( F \subset  {F}^{\prime } \) . Hence for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and \( k \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) large enough,

\[
F = {F}^{\prime }\text{ . }
\]

(6) Since the set \( k \cdot  {T}_{\bar{h}}{C}_{\delta }\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) is bounded, we have that the set \( {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) is bounded. On the other hand, clearly

\[
{F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  \subset  {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\delta /2}\left( {s}_{0}\right)
\]

for any \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) . Hence the set \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right)  = {F}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) \) is bounded for any \( s \) close enough to \( {s}_{0} \) . This contradicts the definition of \( {s}_{0} \) since there exists a sequence \( {\left\{  {s}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  \mathbb{N}} \) with \( {s}_{i} \rightarrow  {s}_{0} \) such that \( F \smallsetminus  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( {s}_{i}\right) \) is not bounded for all \( i \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_title: ODE–PDE Maximum Principle for Invariant Bundle Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \( W \) is a vector bundle over a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , with bundle projection \( \pi  : W \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) , equipped with a fixed fibre metric \( h \) and a smooth family of connections \( A\left( t\right) \) compatible with \( h \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a smooth family of Riemannian metrics on \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

Suppose that \( \Upsilon  \in  \Gamma \left( {{\pi }^{ * }\left( W\right) }\right) \) , that is, \( \Upsilon \) is a vector field on \( W \) which is parallel to the fibres of \( W \) , and that \( X \subset  W \) is a closed subset which is parallel and convex in the sense of Definition 9.5.5, and preserved under the ODE

\[
\frac{de}{dt} = \Upsilon \left( e\right) \tag{9.6.1}
\]

More precisely, if \( e\left( t\right) \) is a solution to (9.6.1) on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\epsilon }\right\rbrack \) , with \( e\left( 0\right)  \in  X \) then we assume that \( e\left( t\right)  \in  X \) for all \( t \) .

Then the set \( X \) is preserved under the PDE

\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{A}E = \Upsilon \left( E\right) \tag{9.6.2}
\]

for \( E\left( t\right)  \in  \Gamma \left( W\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . In other words, if \( E\left( {x,0}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , then \( E\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

Note that the ODE (9.6.1) preserves each fibre.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
First note that we may assume, without loss of generality, that \( X \) is compact. Indeed, if we had a counterexample to the theorem for \( X \) noncompact, then we could intersect \( X \) with the parallel, convex subset

\[
{T}_{r} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \{ w \in  W : \left| w\right|  < r\} , \tag{9.6.3}
\]

for \( r > 0 \) sufficiently large that the image of the counterexample \( E \) always lay within \( {T}_{r/2} \) , and modify \( \Upsilon \) outside the image of \( E \) appropriately to give a counterexample for \( X \) compact. (Here, and throughout the proof, the quantity \( \left| w\right| \) of a point in \( W \) will always be measured with respect to \( h \) .)

Define \( \psi  : W \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by \( \psi \left( w\right)  = \operatorname{dist}\left( {w, X}\right) \) , the fibrewise distance function to the convex set \( X \) , using the fibre metric \( h \) . Define \( Y = \{ w \in  W \mid  \psi \left( w\right)  < 2\} \) , and let \( K \) be the (fibrewise) Lipschitz constant for \( \Upsilon \) within \( Y \) . That is, for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , and for all \( v, w \in  {Y}_{x} \) (the part of \( Y \) in the fibre over \( x \) ) we have

\[
\left| {\Upsilon \left( v\right)  - \Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right|  \leq  K\left| {v - w}\right| . \tag{9.6.4}
\]

For a given \( w \in  Y \smallsetminus  X \) , we pick the point \( p \in  \partial X \) in the same fibre as \( w \) which is closest to \( w \) , and define \( x \mathrel{\text{ := }} \pi \left( w\right) \) . It is also convenient to highlight the linear function \( L : {W}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) defined by \( L\left( v\right)  = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {v - p}\right) \) , and note that

\[
L \leq  0\text{ on }{X}_{x};\;L \leq  \psi  \leq  \operatorname{dist}\left( {\cdot , p}\right) \text{ near }w\text{ in }{W}_{x}. \tag{9.6.5}
\]

By the ODE hypothesis, we must have

\[
d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  \leq  0. \tag{9.6.6}
\]

If not, we would solve the ODE (9.6.1) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) to find that

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}L\left( e\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0} = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  > 0,
\]

which, by (9.6.5), would make \( \psi \left( {e\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  L\left( {e\left( t\right) }\right)  > 0 \) for small \( t > 0 \) , a contradiction.

The inequality (9.6.6) then leads to

(9.6.7)

\[
d{\psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right)  - \Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  + d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left| {\Upsilon \left( w\right)  - \Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right|  \leq  {K\psi }\left( w\right) ,
\]

for our arbitrary point \( w \in  Y \smallsetminus  X \) .

In order to apply the maximum principle as we stated it in Chapter 3, it will be convenient to work with a slightly smoothed version of \( \psi \) . Since \( \psi \) is \( {C}^{1} \) on \( Y \smallsetminus  X \) (recall (9.6.5)) for any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) , we can mollify \( \psi \) (see [15]) by a small amount (depending on \( \varepsilon \) ) on each fibre, using the metric \( h \) , to give a smooth, parallel, convex function \( \Psi  : W \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) for which

\[
\left| {\Psi  - \psi }\right|  < \varepsilon
\]

on \( Y \) , and

\[
d{\Psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  \leq  {2K\Psi }\left( w\right) \tag{9.6.8}
\]

on the set \( \{ w \in  W \mid  \Psi \left( w\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\varepsilon }{2},1}\right\rbrack  \}  \subset  Y \) .

Now let us take a solution \( E \) to the PDE as in the theorem. We will constraint the evolution of \( E \) by applying the maximum principle to \( u \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \Psi  \circ  E : \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) . By Proposition 9.5.4 and (9.6.8), we have

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{\mathcal{M}}}\right) u\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  d{\Psi }_{x}\left( {E\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( {E\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) }\right)  \leq  {2Ku}\left( {x, t}\right) \tag{9.6.9}
\]

whenever \( u\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\varepsilon }{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, if we choose some smooth \( F : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) for which \( F\left( v\right)  = 2\widetilde{Kv} \) for \( v \geq  \varepsilon \) , and so that \( d{\Psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  \leq  F\left( {\Psi \left( w\right) }\right) \) for all \( w \in  W \) with \( \Psi \left( w\right)  \leq  1 \) , then

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{\mathcal{M}}}\right) u \leq  F\left( u\right) \tag{9.6.10}
\]

for sufficiently small \( t \) so that \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  1 \) . This is the equation to which we can apply Theorem 3.1.1. Noting that \( u\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  \leq  \varepsilon \) , we compare \( u \) to the function \( \phi \left( t\right)  = \varepsilon {e}^{2Kt} \) , and find that for \( \varepsilon  < {e}^{-{2KT}} \) , we have \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {e}^{2Kt} \leq  \varepsilon {e}^{2KT} < 1 \) , the last of these inequalities being mentioned to emphasise that we need not worry about (9.6.10) failing to hold before time \( T \) . Returning from \( \Psi \) to \( \psi \) , we find that \( \psi  \circ  E \leq  \Psi  \circ  E + \varepsilon  = u + \varepsilon \) , and hence that

\[
\psi  \circ  E \leq  \varepsilon \left( {{e}^{2KT} + 1}\right)
\]

on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . This last inequality is independent of the mollification, and holds for all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , and hence \( \psi  \circ  E \equiv  0 \) throughout, which is equivalent to having \( E\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) as desired.

The only aspect of the ODE hypothesis that we used in the proof is the following property: For all \( p \in  \partial X \) , when we solve the ODE (9.6.1) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) , then

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}L\left( e\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0} \leq  0 \tag{9.6.11}
\]

whenever \( L : {W}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a nonconstant linear function such that \( L\left( p\right)  = 0 \) and \( L \leq  0 \) on \( X \) . This property could be shown to be equivalent to the ODE hypothesis, although one should beware of the subtlety that if we only knew that for some \( p \in  \partial X \) , the ODE solution \( e\left( t\right) \) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) satisfied (9.6.11) for all \( L \) as before, then it could still be the case that \( e\left( t\right)  \notin  X \) for all \( t > 0 \) even though \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \in  X \) .

At \( t = 0 \) , we have \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\beta g} > 0 \) . In terms of the eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{i} \) , this may be phrased

\[
{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \beta  > 0
\]

We define a first convex parallel function to be

\[
{\Psi }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \beta  - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)
\]

which will be weakly negative at \( t = 0 \) . We also see readily that the weak negativity of \( {\Psi }_{1} \) is preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Returning to \( t = 0 \) , combining the facts \( {\beta g} \leq \) Ric and \( R \leq  {3B} \) tells us that Ric \( \geq  \frac{\beta }{3B}{Rg} \) . After defining \( \varepsilon  = \frac{\beta }{3B} \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{3}}\right) \) , and \( \delta  = \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }} \in  \left( {0,2}\right) \) , we know from the proof of Theorem 9.7.5 that this condition is equivalent to

\[
{\Psi }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \leq  0, \tag{9.7.6}
\]

and is also preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Set \( \theta  = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta } \in  \left( {\frac{1}{2},1}\right) \) . Note that at \( t = 0,{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} + \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \; {\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  \leq  B \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{3}}\right)  \geq  \beta \) . Hence, by choosing \( A > 0 \) sufficiently large (depending on \( \beta \) and \( B \) ) we have

\[
{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }, \tag{9.7.7}
\]

at \( t = 0 \) .

We claim that (9.7.7) is preserved under our Ricci flow. If this were true, then by Remark 9.7.9 we would have

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}\right) }^{\theta } = \widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta }
\]

for \( \widetilde{A} = \widetilde{A}\left( {\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} A{2}^{-\theta } \) . The theorem would then hold with

\[
M = M\left( {\gamma ,\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{R \geq  0}}\left( {\widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta } - {\gamma R}}\right)  < \infty .
\]

It remains to show that (9.7.7) is preserved under this Ricci flow. By Lemma 9.7.2, \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \) is convex, \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) is concave and \( {\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \) is concave where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) . Therefore,

\[
{\Psi }_{3} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }
\]

is a convex function where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) , and in particular, where \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) .

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) consisting of all points where \( {\Psi }_{1},{\Psi }_{2} \) and \( {\Psi }_{3} \) are all weakly negative. The theorem tells us that the set \( X \) is preserved under the Ricci flow (and in particular that (9.7.7) will continue to hold) provided that \( X \) is preserved under the analogous ODE (9.6.1), or equivalently (9.7.1).

We have already remarked that both the conditions \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) are preserved under the ODE (9.7.1). We will conclude by showing that if our eigenvalues solve (9.7.1) and satisfy \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) , then whenever \( {\Psi }_{3} \geq  0 \) , the ratio \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing in time.

In this case, our eigenvalues satisfy \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} > 0 \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} > 0 \) , and we may calculate that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2} - {\lambda }_{1}^{2} - {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)  = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

and that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{3} + \frac{{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack   = 2\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  + \frac{2{\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Now \( \delta {\lambda }_{3} \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) (since \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) ) and \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{2} \) , so

\[
\delta \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \frac{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}} \leq  \frac{{\left( 2{\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) .
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left\lbrack  \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }}\right\rbrack   \leq  2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - {2\theta }\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) \left( {1 - \theta \left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= 0
\]

by definition of \( \theta \) . Therefore, \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing as claimed, and (9.7.7) is preserved.

As before, we study the ODE system

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} \frac{d\lambda }{dt} = {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \nu }, \\  \frac{d\mu }{dt} = {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda \nu }, \\  \frac{d\nu }{dt} = {\nu }^{2} + {\lambda \mu }. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider again the function

\[
y = f\left( x\right)  = x\left( {\log x - 3}\right)
\]

for \( {e}^{2} \leq  x <  + \infty \) , which is increasing and convex with range \( - {e}^{2} \leq  y <  + \infty \) . Its inverse function \( x = {f}^{-1}\left( y\right) \) is increasing and concave on \( - {e}^{2} \leq  y <  + \infty \) . For each \( t \geq  0 \) , we consider the set \( K\left( t\right) \) of \( 3 \times  3 \) symmetric matrices defined by the inequalities:

(5.3.1)

\[
\lambda  + \mu  + \nu  \geq   - \frac{3}{1 + t}
\]

and

(5.3.2)

\[
\nu \left( {1 + t}\right)  + {f}^{-1}\left( {\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \nu }\right) \left( {1 + t}\right) }\right)  \geq  0,
\]

which is closed and convex (as we saw in the proof of Theorem 2.4.1). By the assumptions at \( t = 0 \) and the advanced maximum principle Theorem 2.3.5, we only need to check that the set \( K\left( t\right) \) is preserved by the ODE system.

Since \( R = \lambda  + \mu  + \nu \) , we get from the ODE that

\[
\frac{dR}{dt} \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}^{2} \geq  \frac{1}{3}{R}^{2}
\]

which implies that

\[
R \geq   - \frac{3}{1 + t},\;\text{ for all }t \geq  0.
\]

Thus the first inequality (5.3.1) is preserved. Note that the second inequality (5.3.2) is automatically satisfied when \( \left( {-\nu }\right)  \leq  3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) . Now we compute from the ODE system,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\frac{R}{\left( -\nu \right) } - \log \left( {-\nu }\right) }\right)  = \frac{1}{{\left( -\nu \right) }^{2}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {-\nu }\right)  \cdot  \frac{dR}{dt} - \left( {R + \left( {-\nu }\right) }\right) \frac{d\left( {-\nu }\right) }{dt}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\left( -\nu \right) }^{2}}\left\lbrack  {{\left( -\nu \right) }^{3} + \left( {-\nu }\right) {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda }^{2}\left( {\left( {-\nu }\right)  + \mu }\right)  - {\lambda \mu }\left( {\nu  - \mu }\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {-\nu }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{3}{\left( 1 + t\right) }
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack  {\log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack
\]

whenever \( R = \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack \) and \( \left( {-\nu }\right)  \geq  3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) . Thus the second inequality (5.3.2) is also preserved under the system of ODE.

Therefore we have proved the theorem.

Then \( \widehat{S} \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
In view of condition (iii), \( \widehat{R} \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Therefore, the assertion is true for \( \widehat{b} = 0 \) . Hence, it suffices to consider the case \( 0 < \widehat{b} \leq  \delta {e}^{-8\widehat{t}} \) . Let us define functions \( a\left( t\right) , b\left( t\right) \) by \( b\left( t\right)  = {e}^{8\left( {\widehat{t} - t}\right) }\widehat{b} \) and \( a\left( t\right)  = {2b}\left( t\right)  + \left( {n - 2}\right) b{\left( t\right) }^{2} \) . Moreover, let \( S\left( t\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\ell }_{a\left( t\right) , b\left( t\right) }^{-1}\left( {R\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since condition (i) holds up to time \( \widehat{t} \) , we know that \( S\left( t\right)  \in \) PIC for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack \) . The evolution of \( S\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}S\left( t\right) \right| }_{t = \widehat{t}} = Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - {b}^{\prime }\left( \widehat{t}\right) U = Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U,
\]

where

\[
U = \frac{1}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{n}\left( {\frac{1}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}} - \frac{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) \widehat{b}}{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \widehat{a}}}\right) \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \text{ id } \oslash  \text{ id. }
\]

We claim that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. To verify this, we distinguish two cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) is strictly two-positive. By Lemma A.2, \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Since \( 2\widehat{a} = 2\widehat{b} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\widehat{b}}^{2} \) , this implies that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Since \( U \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC by Lemma 2.5, it follows that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC, as claimed.

Case 2: Suppose next that \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) is not strictly two-positive. In this case, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \leq  C\left( n\right) \left| {\mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right| \) . Since \( 2\widehat{a} = 2\widehat{b} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\widehat{b}}^{2} \) , it follows that

\[
{D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - 2\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  - 2{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  \mathrm{{PIC}}
\]

if \( \widehat{b} > 0 \) is sufficiently small. Condition (ii) implies \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \) id is weakly two-positive. Using Lemma A.2, we obtain

\[
2\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)
\]

\[
+ 4\widehat{a}\left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} + 4\widehat{a}\left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}}\right) \mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

\[
= 2\widehat{a}\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \mathrm{{id}}}\right\rbrack   \oslash  \left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + \left( {1 + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right) \mathrm{{id}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ 2\widehat{a}{\left( 1 - {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  \text{ PIC. }
\]

On the other hand, Lemma 2.6 gives

\[
8\widehat{b}U - 4\widehat{a}\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} + {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}}\mathrm{{PIC}}\text{ . }
\]

Moreover, if \( \widehat{b} > 0 \) is sufficiently small, then \( \widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}} \) is much smaller than \( {\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}} \) . Since \( \left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \) , it follows that

\[
{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{17}{8}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( S\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{4}}\operatorname{scal}\left( \widehat{S}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - 4\widehat{a}{\widehat{b}}^{\frac{5}{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( \widehat{S}\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}
\]

lies in the interior of the PIC cone. Adding all four formulae, we conclude that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC.

To summarize, we have shown that \( {D}_{\widehat{a},\widehat{b}}\left( \widehat{S}\right)  + 8\widehat{b}U \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. Since \( Q\left( \widehat{S}\right)  \in  {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC by Proposition 7.5 in [5], we conclude that \( {\left. \frac{d}{dt}S\left( t\right) \right| }_{t = \widehat{t}} \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{\widehat{S}} \) PIC. Hence, if \( \widehat{S} \) lies on the boundary of the PIC cone, then \( S\left( t\right) \) lies outside the PIC cone if \( t \in  \lbrack 0,\widehat{t}) \) is sufficiently close to \( \widehat{t} \) . This is a contradiction. This completes the proof of Lemma 2.7.

keywords: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions

knowledge_statements.title: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_title: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algebraic curvature operator \( R \) is said to be WPIC (weakly positive isotropic curvature) if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) , we have

\[
{R}_{1313} + {R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {R}_{2424} - 2{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.1}
\]

\( R \) is said to be WPIC1 if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.2}
\]

Moreover \( R \) is said to be WPIC2 if for any orthonormal 4-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) .

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {\mu }^{2}{R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.3}
\]

We call \( {C}_{PIC},{C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC2} \) the cones consisting of algebraic curvature operators that satisfy WPIC, WPIC1 or WPIC2 respectively. Moreover, \( R \) is said to be PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 if it’s contained in the interior of \( {C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC1} \) or \( {C}_{PIC2} \) respectively. A manifold \( M \) is a PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 manifold if there exists a metric \( g \) on \( M \) such that its curvature operator is PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 respectively.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  (0, T\rbrack \) , be a complete solution to the Ricci flow (possibly with unbounded curvature). Moreover, we assume that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and strictly PIC. Suppose that there exists a point \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) in space-time with the property that the curvature tensor at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) lies on the boundary of the PIC2 cone. Then, for each \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) , the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits off a line.
