knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies the Harnack inequality, it suffices to show that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature. The proof is by contradiction. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature.

By the strict maximum principle, we can find a real number \( \delta  > 0 \) with the property that the scalar curvature \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is strictly positive for \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) .

Consequently, \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC for \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) . We distinguish two cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC2. In this case, \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) by the soul theorem (cf. [10]). By a standard point-picking argument, there exists a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  M \) such that \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  {j}^{4} \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies the Harnack inequality, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-4{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

Using Shi's interior derivative estimate, we obtain bounds for all the derivatives of curvature on \( {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, j{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . We now dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . Using the noncollapsing assumption and the curvature derivative estimates, we conclude that, after passing to a subsequence, the rescaled flows converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a smooth nonflat ancient solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . The limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. By Proposition 6.8, the manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. By Corollary 6.7, universal cover of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a family of shrinking cylinders \( {S}^{n - 1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Therefore, \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a quotient \( \left( {{S}^{n - 1}/\Gamma }\right)  \times  \mathbb{R} \) . If \( \Gamma \) is nontrivial, then a result of Hamilton implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form \( {S}^{n - 1}/\Gamma \) (cf. [6, Th. A.2]), but this is impossible since \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Thus, \( \Gamma \) is trivial, and \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a standard cylinder \( {S}^{n - 1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Consequently, \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 . This contradicts Proposition 6.9.

Case 2: Suppose finally that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not strictly PIC2. By Proposition 6.6, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a product \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( t\right) }\right)  \times  \mathbb{R} \) for each \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) . Clearly, \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) , is a complete solution to the Ricci flow of dimension \( n - 1 \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales, weakly PIC2, and uniformly PIC1. By assumption, \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature. Using a point-picking lemma, we can construct a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  X \) such that \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  {j}^{4} \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

As in Case 1, the Harnack inequality and Shi's interior derivative estimate give bounds for all the derivatives of curvature on \( {B}_{{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, j{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we obtain a smooth nonflat limit that is uniformly PIC1 and that must split off a line by Proposition 6.8. This is a contradiction.

Thus \( \widetilde{C}\left( t\right)  = \widetilde{C}{\left( t\right) }^{\prime } + {W}^{\prime } \) where \( \widetilde{C}{\left( t\right) }^{\prime } \subset  {W}^{\prime  \bot  } \cap  \operatorname{Fix}\left( {-\mathrm{{id}}}\right) \) is convex.

We may assume that the norm of \( {\mathrm{{Hk}}}_{\mid \mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right)  \times  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) } \) is bounded by some a priori constant for all \( \mathrm{{Hk}} \in  C\left( t\right) \) . This in turn implies that a sequence in \( \widetilde{C}{\left( t\right) }^{\prime } \) tends to \( \infty \) if and only if its trace is unbounded.

Using that \( \widetilde{C}\left( t\right) \) is invariant under the ODE and that \( {C}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) has full dimension it is easy to see that for all positive \( t \) there are endomorphisms with arbitrary small as well as endomorphisms with arbitrary large trace in \( \widetilde{C}\left( t\right) \) and hence in \( \widetilde{C}{\left( t\right) }^{\prime } \) . Therefore \( W \subset  {\partial }_{\infty }\widetilde{C}\left( t\right) \) . This implies as before \( V \subset  {\partial }_{\infty }C\left( t\right) \) for all positive \( t \) as claimed.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex: By the soul theorem (cf. [10]), \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . By the solution of the Schoenflies conjecture in dimension \( n \geq  5,\sum \) bounds a compact domain \( \Omega \) that is diffeomorphic to \( {B}^{n} \) . Let us choose a diffeomorphism \( F : \Omega  \rightarrow \; {B}^{n} \) , and let \( f : \partial \Omega  \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) be an \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) -isometry. Without loss of generality, we may assume that the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} : {S}^{n - 1} \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) is orientation-preserving. We claim that the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} : {S}^{n - 1} \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) is isotopic to the identity. To prove this, let \( z \) denote the height function on the neck \( N \) , so that \( \{ z = 0\}  = \sum \) and \( \{ z \in  \lbrack  - {10},0)\}  \subset  \Omega \) . Moreover, let \( \varphi \left( z\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{1}{z}} \) for \( z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Let us define a modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) as follows. The metric \( \widetilde{g} \) agrees with \( g \) inside \( \Omega \) . In the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{20}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , we change the metric conformally by \( \widetilde{g} = {e}^{-{2\varphi }}g \) . In the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , we define \( \widetilde{g} = {e}^{-{2\varphi }}\left( {\chi \left( z\right) g + \left( {1 - \chi \left( z\right) }\right) \bar{g}}\right) \) , where \( \bar{g} \) denotes the standard metric on the cylinder and \( \chi  : \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) is a smooth cutoff function satisfying \( \chi \left( z\right)  = 1 \) for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{18}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \chi \left( z\right)  = 0 \) for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the original metric \( g \) is strictly PIC2, the modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) will be strictly PIC2 in the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . Moreover, the surgically modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) is rotationally symmetric for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Consequently, we can extend \( \widetilde{g} \) by gluing in a rotationally symmetric cap. This can be done in such a way that the glued metric is strictly PIC2. To summarize, we obtain a closed manifold that is obtained by gluing two balls, and that admits a metric that is strictly PIC2. If the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} \) is not isotopic to the identity, then this glued manifold is an exotic sphere, that contradicts the fact that exotic spheres do not admit metrics that are strictly PIC2 (cf. [8]).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  (0, T\rbrack \) , be a complete solution to the Ricci flow (possibly with unbounded curvature). Moreover, we assume that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and strictly PIC. Suppose that there exists a point \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) in space-time with the property that the curvature tensor at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) lies on the boundary of the PIC2 cone. Then, for each \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) , the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits off a line.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Suppose that the assertion is false. Then there exists a time \( \tau  \in \; \left( {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) with the property that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) does not split off a line. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, we conclude that \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally irreducible. In view of Berger's holonomy classification theorem, there are four possible cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = {SO}\left( n\right) \) . If we fix an arbitrary pair of real numbers \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , then Theorem 9.13 in [5] implies that the set of all orthonormal four-frames \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) satisfying

\[
{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  = 0
\]

is invariant under parallel transport. Since \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = {SO}\left( n\right) \) , we conclude that

\[
{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  > 0
\]

for all orthonormal four-frames \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and all \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . In other words, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC2 cone.

Let \( \Omega \) be a bounded open neighborhood of the point \( {p}_{0} \) with smooth boundary. Let us choose a smooth function \( f : \bar{\Omega } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with the property that \( f > 0 \) in \( \Omega , f = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \) , and \( {R}_{g\left( \tau \right) } - \frac{1}{2}f \) id \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC2. Let \( F \) : \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) denote the solution of the linear heat equation with respect to the evolving metric \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial data \( F\left( {\cdot ,\tau }\right)  = f \) and Dirichlet boundary condition \( F = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( S \mathrel{\text{ := }} {R}_{g\left( t\right) } - \frac{1}{2}F\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) id \( \oslash \) id. Then \( {D}_{t}S = {\Delta S} + Q\left( S\right)  + {2F}\operatorname{Ric}\left( S\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{id} + \left( {n - 1}\right) {F}^{2}\operatorname{id} \oslash  \operatorname{id} \) . Using the maximum principle, we conclude that \( {R}_{g\left( t\right) } - \frac{1}{2}F\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) id \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC2 at each point in \( \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( F\left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  > 0 \) , the curvature tensor at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC2 cone, contrary to our assumption.

Case 2: Suppose that \( n = {2m} \) and \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = U\left( m\right) \) . In this case, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a Kähler manifold. This is impossible since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC.

Case 3: Suppose next that \( n = {4m} \geq  8 \) and \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = \operatorname{Sp}\left( m\right) \) . \( \mathrm{{Sp}}\left( 1\right) \) . In this case, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a quaternionic Kähler manifold. In particular, \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is an Einstein manifold. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, we conclude that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a round sphere (cf. [4]). This is impossible.

Case 4: Suppose finally that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  \neq  {SO}\left( n\right) \) and \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally symmetric. In this case, \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is an Einstein manifold, for otherwise the eigenspaces of the Ricci tensor give a splitting of the tangent bundle into parallel subbundles, which is impossible since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally irreducible. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, it follows that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a round sphere (cf. [4]). This contradicts the fact that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  \neq  {SO}\left( n\right) \) . This completes the proof of Theorem 6.6.

(Hamilton [65]). Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , be a noncollapsing nonsingular solution of the normalized Ricci flow on a compact three-manifold \( M \) . Then either

(i) there exist a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{k} : M \rightarrow  M \) so that the pull-back of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{k} \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to a metric on \( M \) with constant sectional curvature; or

(ii) we can find a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, and for all \( t \) beyond some time \( T <  + \infty \) we can find compact subsets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) respectively obtained by truncating each cusp of the hyperbolic manifolds along constant mean curvature torus of small area, and diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) ,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , of \( {K}_{l} \) into \( M \) so that as long as \( t \) sufficiently large, the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close as to the hyperbolic metric as we like on the compact sets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) ; and moreover if we call the exceptional part of \( M \) those points where they are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) , we can take the injectivity radii of the exceptional part at everywhere as small as we like and the boundary tori of each \( {K}_{l} \) are incompressible in the sense that each \( {\varphi }_{l} \) injects \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {K}_{l}}\right) \) into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. We will divide the proof into three parts.

## Part I: Subsequence Convergence

According to Lemma 5.1.1, the scalar curvature of the normalized flow evolves by the equation

(5.3.3)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| Ric\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{rR}
\]

\[
= {\Delta R} + 2\left| \mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\right|  + \frac{2}{3}R\left( {R - r}\right)
\]

where \( \overset{ \circ  }{Ric} \) is the traceless part of the Ricci tensor. As before, we denote by \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = \; \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) . It then follows from the maximum principle that

(5.3.4)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min } \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }\left( {{R}_{\min } - r}\right) ,
\]

which implies that if \( {R}_{\min } \leq  0 \) it must be nondecreasing, and if \( {R}_{\min } \geq  0 \) it cannot go negative again. We can then divide the noncollapsing solutions of the normalized Ricci flow into three cases.

Case (1): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  > 0 \) for some \( t > 0 \) ; Case (2): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) ; Case (3): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  < 0 \) .

Let us first consider Case (1). In this case the maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) of the corresponding solution of the unnormalized flow is finite, since the unnormalized scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \) satisfies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{R} = \Delta \widetilde{R} + 2{\left| \widetilde{R}ic\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  \Delta \widetilde{R} + \frac{2}{3}{\widetilde{R}}^{2}
\]

which implies that the curvature of the unnormalized solution blows up in finite time. Without loss of generality, we may assume that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator are bounded below by \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that the pinching estimate

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack
\]

holds whenever \( \widetilde{\nu } < 0 \) . This shows that when the unnormalized curvature big, the negative ones are not nearly as large as the positive ones. Note that the unnormalized curvature becomes unbounded in finite time. Thus when we rescale the unnormalized flow to the normalized flow, the scaling factor must go to infinity. In the nonsingular case the rescaled positive curvature stay finite, so the rescaled negative curvature (if any) go to zero. Hence we can take a noncollapsing limit for the nonsingular solution of the normalized flow so that it has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Since the volume of the limit is finite, it follows from a result of Calabi and Yau [112] that the limit must be compact and the limiting manifold is the original one. Then by the strong maximum principle as in the proof of Theorem 5.2.3 (i), either the limit is flat, or it is a compact metric quotient of the product of a positively curved surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. By the work of Schoen-Yau [110], a flat three-manifold cannot have a metric of positive scalar curvature, but our manifold does in Case (1). This rules out the possibility of a flat limit. Clearly the limit is also a nonsingular solution to the normalized Ricci flow. Note that the curvature of the surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) has a positive lower bound and is compact since it comes from the lifting of the compact limiting manifold. From Theorem 5.1.11, we see the metric of the two-dimensional factor \( {\sum }^{2} \) converges to the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the normalized Ricci flow. Note also that the normalized factors in two-dimension and three-dimension are different. This implies that the compact quotient of the product \( {\sum }^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) cannot be nonsingular, which is also ruled out for the limit. Thus the limit must have strictly positive sectional curvature. Since the convergence takes place everywhere for the compact limit, it follows that as \( t \) large enough the original nonsingular solution has strictly positive sectional curvature. This in turn shows that the corresponding unnormalized flow has strictly positive sectional curvature after some finite time. Then in views of the proof of Theorem 5.2.1, in particular the pinching estimate in Proposition 5.2.5, the limit has constant Ricci curvature and then constant sectional curvature for three-manifolds. This finishes the proof in Case (1).

We next consider Case (2). In this case we only need to show that we can take a noncollapsing limit which has nonnegative sectional curvature. Indeed, if this is true, then as in the previous case, the limit is compact and either it is flat, or it splits as a product (or a quotient of a product) of a positively curved \( {S}^{2} \) with a circle \( {S}^{1} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. But the assumption \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all times \( t \geq  0 \) in this case implies the limit must be flat.

Let us consider the corresponding unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) associated to the non-collapsing nonsingular solution. The pinching estimate in Theorem 5.3.2 tells us that we may assume the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) exists for all times \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , for otherwise, the scaling factor approaches infinity as in the previous case which implies the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. The volume \( \widetilde{V}\left( t\right) \) of the unnormalized solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) now changes. We divide the discussion into three subcases.

Subcase (2.1): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) ;

Subcase (2.2): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) ;

Subcase (2.3): there exist two positive constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} \) such that \( {C}_{1} \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( t\right)  \leq  {C}_{2} \) for all \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) .

For Subcase (2.1), because

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{V}}{dt} =  - r\widetilde{V}
\]

we have

\[
\log \frac{\widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right) }{\widetilde{V}\left( 0\right) } =  - {\int }_{0}^{{\widetilde{t}}_{k}}r\left( t\right) {dt} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

which implies that there exists another sequence of times, still denoted by \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) , such that \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and \( r\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \leq  0 \) . Let \( {t}_{k} \) be the corresponding times for the normalized flow. Thus there holds for the normalized flow

\[
r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }\;k \rightarrow  \infty ,
\]

since \( 0 \geq  r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Then

\[
{\int }_{M}\left( {R - {R}_{\min }}\right) {d\mu }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \left( {r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) V \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

As we take a noncollapsing limit along the time sequence \( {t}_{k} \) , we get

\[
{\int }_{{M}^{\infty }}{Rd}{\mu }^{\infty } = 0
\]

for the limit of the normalized solutions at the new time \( t = 0 \) . But \( R \geq  0 \) for the limit because \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) for the nonsingular solution. So \( R = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) for the limit. Since the limit flow exists for \( - \infty  < t <  + \infty \) and the scalar curvature of the limit flow evolves by

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{r}^{\infty }R,\;t \in  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right)

where \( {r}^{\infty } \) is the limit of the function \( r\left( t\right) \) by translating the times \( {t}_{k} \) as the new time \( t = 0 \) . It follows from the strong maximum principle that

\[
R \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

This in turn implies, in view of the above evolution equation, that

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

Hence this limit must be flat. Since the limit \( {M}^{\infty } \) is complete and has finite volume, the flat manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must be compact. Thus the underlying manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must agree with the original \( M \) (as a topological manifold). This says that the limit was taken on \( M \) .

For Subcase (2.2), we may assume as before that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) of the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator satisfy \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It then follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack  ,\;\text{ for all }t \geq  0
\]

whenever \( \widetilde{\nu } < 0 \) .

Let \( {t}_{k} \) be the sequence of times in the normalized flow which corresponds to the sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) . Take a noncollapsing limit for the normalized flow along the times \( {t}_{k} \) . Since \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) , the normalized curvatures at the times \( {t}_{k} \) are reduced by multiplying the factor \( {\left( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \) . For Subcase (2.3), normalizing the flow only changes quantities in a bounded way. As before we have the pinching estimate

\[
R \geq  \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - C}\right\rbrack

for the normalized Ricci flow, where \( C \) is a positive constant depending only on the constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} \) in the assumption of Subcase (2.3). If

\[
\left( {-\nu }\right)  \leq  \frac{A}{1 + t}
\]

for any fixed positive constant \( A \) , then \( \left( {-\nu }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) and we can take a noncollapsing limit which has nonnegative sectional curvature. On the other hand if we can pick a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and points \( {x}_{k} \) where \( \left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \; \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfies

\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \left( {1 + {t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty ,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

then from the pinching estimate, we have

\[
\frac{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }{\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) } \rightarrow   + \infty ,\;\text{ as }\;k \rightarrow   + \infty .

We now come to the most interesting Case (3) where \( {R}_{\min } \) increases monotonically to a limit strictly less than zero. By scaling we can assume \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

\[

for any convergent subsequence. And since

\[
{\int }_{M}\left( {R - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {d\mu } = \left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)  \cdot  V,

Thus the limit metric has \( \lambda  = \mu  = \nu  =  - 2 \) , so it has constant sectional curvature -1 as desired. 0

Now we first want to find a finite collection of persistent complete noncompact hyperbolic manifolds as stated in Theorem 5.3.4 (ii).

## Part II: Persistence of Hyperbolic Pieces

We begin with the definition of the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for maps \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) of one Riemannian manifold to another. For any compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) and any two maps \( F, G : M \rightarrow  N \) , we define

\[
{d}_{K}\left( {F, G}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  K}}d\left( {F\left( x\right) , G\left( x\right) }\right)
\]

where \( d\left( {y, z}\right) \) is the geodesic distance from \( y \) to \( z \) on \( N \) . This gives the \( {C}_{loc}^{0} \) topology for maps between \( M \) and \( N \) . To define \( {C}_{loc}^{k} \) topology for any positive integer \( k \geq  1 \) , we consider the \( k \) -jet space \( {J}^{k}M \) of a manifold \( M \) which is the collection of all

\[
\left( {x,{J}^{1},{J}^{2},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)
\]

where \( x \) is a point on \( M \) and \( {J}^{i} \) is a tangent vector for \( 1 \leq  i \leq  k \) defined by the \( {i}^{th} \) covariant derivative \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) \) for a path \( \gamma \) passing through the point \( x \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . A smooth map \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) induces a map

\[
{J}^{k}F : \;{J}^{k}M \rightarrow  {J}^{k}N
\]

defined by

\[
{J}^{k}F\left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)  = \left( {F\left( x\right) ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{k}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \gamma \) is a path passing through the point \( x \) with \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) ,1 \leq  i \leq  k \) .

Define the k-jet distance between \( F \) and \( G \) on a compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) by

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) }\left( {F, G}\right)  = {d}_{B{J}^{k}K}\left( {{J}^{k}F,{J}^{k}G}\right)
\]

where \( B{J}^{k}K \) consists of all \( k \) -jets \( \left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right) \) with \( x \in  K \) and

\[
{\left| {J}^{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {J}^{2}\right| }^{2} + \cdots  + {\left| {J}^{k}\right| }^{2} \leq  1
\]

Then the convergence in the metric \( {d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) } \) for all positive integers \( k \) and all compact sets \( K \) defines the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for the space of maps.

We will need the following Mostow type rigidity result.

LEMMA 5.3.7. For any complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) with finite volume with metric \( h \) , we can find a compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) such that for every integer \( k \) and every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist an integer \( q \) and a \( \delta  > 0 \) with the following property: if \( F \) is a diffeomorphism of \( \mathcal{K} \) into another complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), finite volume with metric \( \widetilde{h} \) such that

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}^{ * }\widetilde{h} - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < \delta
\]

then there exists an isometry I of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) such that

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {F, I}\right)  < \varepsilon .
\]

Proof. First we claim that \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) for an appropriate choice of compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) , positive integer \( q \) and positive number \( \delta \) . Let \( l : \mathcal{H} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a function defined at each point by the length of the shortest non-contractible loop starting and ending at this point. Denote the Margulis constant by \( \mu \) . Then by Margulis lemma (see for example [55] or [76]), for any \( 0 < {\varepsilon }_{0} < \frac{1}{2}\mu \) , the set \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  \mathcal{H} \) consists of finitely many components and each of these components is isometric to a cusp or to a tube. Topologically, a tube is just a solid torus. Let \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) be even smaller than one half of the minimum of the lengths of the all closed geodesics on the tubes. Then \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) consists of finite number of cusps. Set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} = {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{\varepsilon }_{0},\infty }\right) \right) \) . The boundary of \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) consists of flat tori with constant mean curvatures. Note that each embedded torus in a complete hyperbolic three-manifold with finite volume either bounds a solid torus or is isotopic to a standard torus in a cusp. The diffeomorphism \( F \) implies the boundary \( F\left( {\partial {\mathcal{K}}_{0}}\right) \) are embedded tori. If one of components bounds a solid torus, then as \( \delta \) sufficiently small and \( q \) sufficiently large, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) would have fewer cusps than \( \mathcal{H} \) , which contradicts with our assumption. Consequently, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( F\left( {\mathcal{K}}_{0}\right) \) . Here \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) is the interior of the set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) . Since \( \mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0},\mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . Hence by Mostow’s rigidity theorem (see [97] and [107]), \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) .

So we can assume \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \mathcal{H} \) . For \( \mathcal{K} = {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) , we argue by contradiction. Suppose there is some \( k > 0 \) and \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) so that there exist sequences of integers \( {q}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty ,{\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) and diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{j} \) mapping \( \mathcal{K} \) into \( \mathcal{H} \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{j}^{ * }h - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{j}}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < {\delta }_{j}
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {{F}_{j}, I}\right)  \geq  \varepsilon
\]

for all isometries \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to itself. We can extract a subsequence of \( {F}_{j} \) convergent to a map \( {F}_{\infty } \) with \( {F}_{\infty }^{ * }h = h \) on \( \mathcal{K} \) .

We need to check that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is still a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism and is the limit of diffeomorphisms, we can find an inverse of \( {F}_{\infty } \) on \( {F}_{\infty }\left( \mathcal{K}\right) \) . So \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . We claim the image of the boundary can not touch the image of the interior. Indeed, if \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{1}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{2}\right) \) with \( {x}_{1} \in  \partial \mathcal{K} \) and \( {x}_{2} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) , then we can find \( {x}_{3} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{4} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{2} \) with \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{3}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{4}\right) \) , since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism. This contradicts with the fact that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . This proves our claim. Hence, the only possible overlap is at the boundary. But the image \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {\partial \mathcal{K}}\right) \) is strictly concave, this prevents the boundary from touching itself. We conclude that the mapping \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) , hence an isometry.

To extend \( {F}_{\infty } \) to a global isometry, we argue as follows. For each truncated cusp end of \( \mathcal{K} \) , the area of constant mean curvature flat torus is strictly decreasing. Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes each such torus to another of the same area, we see that \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes the foliation of an end by constant mean curvature flat tori to another such foliation. So \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes cusps to cusps and preserves their foliations. Note that the isometric type of a cusp is just the isometric type of the torus, more precisely, let \( \left( {N, d{r}^{2} + {e}^{-{2r}}{g}_{\mathcal{V}}}\right) \) be a cusp (where \( {g}_{\mathcal{V}} \) is the flat metric on the torus \( \mathcal{V} \) ), \( 0 < a < b \) are two constants, any isometry of \( N \cap  {l}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) to itself is just an isometry of \( \mathcal{V} \) . Hence the isometry \( {F}_{\infty } \) can be extended to the whole cusps. This gives a global isometry \( I \) contradicting our assumption when \( j \) large enough.
