## Part II: Persistence of Hyperbolic Pieces

We begin with the definition of the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for maps \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) of one Riemannian manifold to another. For any compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) and any two maps \( F, G : M \rightarrow  N \) , we define

\[
{d}_{K}\left( {F, G}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  K}}d\left( {F\left( x\right) , G\left( x\right) }\right)
\]

where \( d\left( {y, z}\right) \) is the geodesic distance from \( y \) to \( z \) on \( N \) . This gives the \( {C}_{loc}^{0} \) topology for maps between \( M \) and \( N \) . To define \( {C}_{loc}^{k} \) topology for any positive integer \( k \geq  1 \) , we consider the \( k \) -jet space \( {J}^{k}M \) of a manifold \( M \) which is the collection of all

\[
\left( {x,{J}^{1},{J}^{2},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)
\]

where \( x \) is a point on \( M \) and \( {J}^{i} \) is a tangent vector for \( 1 \leq  i \leq  k \) defined by the \( {i}^{th} \) covariant derivative \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) \) for a path \( \gamma \) passing through the point \( x \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . A smooth map \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) induces a map

\[
{J}^{k}F : \;{J}^{k}M \rightarrow  {J}^{k}N
\]

defined by

\[
{J}^{k}F\left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)  = \left( {F\left( x\right) ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{k}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \gamma \) is a path passing through the point \( x \) with \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) ,1 \leq  i \leq  k \) .

Define the k-jet distance between \( F \) and \( G \) on a compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) by

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) }\left( {F, G}\right)  = {d}_{B{J}^{k}K}\left( {{J}^{k}F,{J}^{k}G}\right)
\]

where \( B{J}^{k}K \) consists of all \( k \) -jets \( \left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right) \) with \( x \in  K \) and

\[
{\left| {J}^{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {J}^{2}\right| }^{2} + \cdots  + {\left| {J}^{k}\right| }^{2} \leq  1
\]

Then the convergence in the metric \( {d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) } \) for all positive integers \( k \) and all compact sets \( K \) defines the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for the space of maps.

We will need the following Mostow type rigidity result.

LEMMA 5.3.7. For any complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) with finite volume with metric \( h \) , we can find a compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) such that for every integer \( k \) and every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist an integer \( q \) and a \( \delta  > 0 \) with the following property: if \( F \) is a diffeomorphism of \( \mathcal{K} \) into another complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), finite volume with metric \( \widetilde{h} \) such that

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}^{ * }\widetilde{h} - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < \delta
\]

then there exists an isometry I of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) such that

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {F, I}\right)  < \varepsilon .
\]

Proof. First we claim that \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) for an appropriate choice of compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) , positive integer \( q \) and positive number \( \delta \) . Let \( l : \mathcal{H} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a function defined at each point by the length of the shortest non-contractible loop starting and ending at this point. Denote the Margulis constant by \( \mu \) . Then by Margulis lemma (see for example [55] or [76]), for any \( 0 < {\varepsilon }_{0} < \frac{1}{2}\mu \) , the set \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  \mathcal{H} \) consists of finitely many components and each of these components is isometric to a cusp or to a tube. Topologically, a tube is just a solid torus. Let \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) be even smaller than one half of the minimum of the lengths of the all closed geodesics on the tubes. Then \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) consists of finite number of cusps. Set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} = {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{\varepsilon }_{0},\infty }\right) \right) \) . The boundary of \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) consists of flat tori with constant mean curvatures. Note that each embedded torus in a complete hyperbolic three-manifold with finite volume either bounds a solid torus or is isotopic to a standard torus in a cusp. The diffeomorphism \( F \) implies the boundary \( F\left( {\partial {\mathcal{K}}_{0}}\right) \) are embedded tori. If one of components bounds a solid torus, then as \( \delta \) sufficiently small and \( q \) sufficiently large, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) would have fewer cusps than \( \mathcal{H} \) , which contradicts with our assumption. Consequently, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( F\left( {\mathcal{K}}_{0}\right) \) . Here \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) is the interior of the set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) . Since \( \mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0},\mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . Hence by Mostow’s rigidity theorem (see [97] and [107]), \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) .

So we can assume \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \mathcal{H} \) . For \( \mathcal{K} = {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) , we argue by contradiction. Suppose there is some \( k > 0 \) and \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) so that there exist sequences of integers \( {q}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty ,{\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) and diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{j} \) mapping \( \mathcal{K} \) into \( \mathcal{H} \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{j}^{ * }h - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{j}}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < {\delta }_{j}
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {{F}_{j}, I}\right)  \geq  \varepsilon
\]

for all isometries \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to itself. We can extract a subsequence of \( {F}_{j} \) convergent to a map \( {F}_{\infty } \) with \( {F}_{\infty }^{ * }h = h \) on \( \mathcal{K} \) .

We need to check that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is still a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism and is the limit of diffeomorphisms, we can find an inverse of \( {F}_{\infty } \) on \( {F}_{\infty }\left( \mathcal{K}\right) \) . So \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . We claim the image of the boundary can not touch the image of the interior. Indeed, if \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{1}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{2}\right) \) with \( {x}_{1} \in  \partial \mathcal{K} \) and \( {x}_{2} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) , then we can find \( {x}_{3} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{4} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{2} \) with \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{3}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{4}\right) \) , since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism. This contradicts with the fact that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . This proves our claim. Hence, the only possible overlap is at the boundary. But the image \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {\partial \mathcal{K}}\right) \) is strictly concave, this prevents the boundary from touching itself. We conclude that the mapping \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) , hence an isometry.

To extend \( {F}_{\infty } \) to a global isometry, we argue as follows. For each truncated cusp end of \( \mathcal{K} \) , the area of constant mean curvature flat torus is strictly decreasing. Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes each such torus to another of the same area, we see that \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes the foliation of an end by constant mean curvature flat tori to another such foliation. So \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes cusps to cusps and preserves their foliations. Note that the isometric type of a cusp is just the isometric type of the torus, more precisely, let \( \left( {N, d{r}^{2} + {e}^{-{2r}}{g}_{\mathcal{V}}}\right) \) be a cusp (where \( {g}_{\mathcal{V}} \) is the flat metric on the torus \( \mathcal{V} \) ), \( 0 < a < b \) are two constants, any isometry of \( N \cap  {l}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) to itself is just an isometry of \( \mathcal{V} \) . Hence the isometry \( {F}_{\infty } \) can be extended to the whole cusps. This gives a global isometry \( I \) contradicting our assumption when \( j \) large enough.

The proof of the Lemma 5.3.7 is completed. [

Pick a sufficiently small number \( a > 0 \) to truncate cusps so that Lemma 5.3.7 is applicable for the compact set \( \mathcal{K} = {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) . Choose an integer \( {l}_{0} \) large enough and an \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) sufficiently small to guarantee from Lemma 5.3.8 the uniqueness of the identity map \( {Id} \) among maps close to \( {Id} \) as a harmonic map \( F \) from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to itself with taking \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to itself, with the normal derivative of \( F \) at the boundary of the domain normal to the boundary of the target, and with \( {d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {F,{Id}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) . Then choose positive integer \( {q}_{0} \) and small number \( {\delta }_{0} > 0 \) from Lemma 5.3.7 such that if \( \widetilde{F} \) is a diffeomorphism of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into another complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), finite volume with metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) satisfying

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widetilde{F}}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  {\delta }_{0},
\]

then there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) such that

(5.3.8)

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {\widetilde{F}, I}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

And we further require \( {q}_{0} \) and \( {\delta }_{0} \) from Lemma 5.3.8 to guarantee the existence of harmonic diffeomorphism from \( \left( {{\mathcal{H}}_{a},{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}}\right) \) to \( \left( {{\mathcal{H}}_{a},{h}_{ij}}\right) \) for any metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij} \) on \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) with \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  {\delta }_{0} \)

By definition, there exist a sequence of exhausting compact sets \( {U}_{k} \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) (each \( \left. {{U}_{k} \supset  {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k} \) from \( {U}_{k} \) into \( M \) such that \( {F}_{k}\left( P\right)  = {P}_{k} \) and \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{m}\left( {U}_{k}\right) } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) for all positive integers \( m \) . Note that \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is strictly concave and we can foliate a neighborhood of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) with constant mean curvature hypersurfaces where the area \( a \) has a nonzero gradient. As the approximating maps \( {F}_{k} : \left( {{U}_{k},{h}_{ij}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are close enough to isometries on this collar of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) , the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) on \( M \) will also admit a unique constant mean curvature hypersurface with the same area \( a \) near \( {F}_{k}\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right) \) by the inverse function theorem. Thus we can change the map \( {F}_{k} \) by an amount which goes to zero as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) so that now \( {F}_{k}\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) has constant mean curvature with the area \( a \) . Furthermore, by applying Lemma 5.3.8 we can again change \( {F}_{k} \) by an amount which goes to zero as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) so as to make \( {F}_{k} \) a harmonic diffeomorphism and take \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to the constant mean curvature hypersurface \( {F}_{k}\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) and also satisfy the free boundary condition that the normal derivative of \( {F}_{k} \) at the boundary of the domain is normal to the boundary of the target. Hence for arbitrarily given positive integer \( q \geq  {q}_{0} \) and positive number \( \delta  < {\delta }_{0} \) , there exists a positive integer \( {k}_{0} \) such that for the modified harmonic diffeomorphism \( {F}_{k} \) , when \( k \geq  {k}_{0} \) ,

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta .
\]

For each fixed \( k \geq  {k}_{0} \) , by the implicit function theorem we can first find a constant mean curvature hypersurface near \( {F}_{k}\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) in \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for \( t \) close to \( {t}_{k} \) and with the same area for each component since \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is strictly concave and a neighborhood of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is foliated by constant mean curvature hypersurfaces where the area \( a \) has a nonzero gradient and \( {F}_{k} : \left( {{\mathcal{H}}_{a},{h}_{ij}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) is close enough to an isometry and \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) varies smoothly. Then by applying Lemma 5.3.8 we can smoothly continue the harmonic diffeomorphism \( {F}_{k} \) forward in time a little to a family of harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , with \( {F}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \; {F}_{k} \) , where each \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into the constant mean curvature hypersurface we just found in \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \) and satisfies the free boundary condition, and also satisfies

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( t\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta .
\]

We claim that for all sufficiently large \( k \) , we can smoothly extend the harmonic diffeomorphism \( {F}_{k} \) to the family harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) with \( \parallel {F}_{k}^{ * }\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( t\right)  - \; {h}_{ij}{\parallel }_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta \) on a maximal time interval \( {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  {\omega }_{k} \) (or \( {t}_{k} \leq  t < {\omega }_{k} \) when \( \left. {{\omega }_{k} =  + \infty }\right) \) ; and if \( {\omega }_{k} <  + \infty \) , then

(5.3.9)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Clearly the above argument shows that the set of \( t \) where we can extend the harmonic diffeomorphisms as desired is open. To verify claim (5.3.9), we thus only need to show that if we have a family of harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) such as we desire for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t < \omega \left( { <  + \infty }\right) \) , we can take the limit of \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) as \( t \rightarrow  \omega \) to get a harmonic diffeomorphism \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) satisfying

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta ,
\]

and if

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta ,
\]

then we can extend \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) forward in time a little (i.e., we can find a constant mean curvature hypersurface near \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) in \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for each \( t \) close to \( \omega \) and with the same area \( a \) for each component). Note that

(5.3.10)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( t\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta .
\]

for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t < \omega \) and the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  \omega \) are uniformly equivalent. We can find a subsequence \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  \omega \) for which \( {F}_{k}\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) converge to \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) in \( {C}^{q - 1}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) and the limit map has

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q - 1}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta .
\]

We need to check that \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is still a diffeomorphism. We at least know \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is a local diffeomorphism, and \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is the limit of diffeomorphisms, so the only possibility of overlap is at the boundary. Hence we use the fact that \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) is still strictly concave since \( q \) is large and \( \delta \) is small to prevent the boundary from touching itself. Thus \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is a diffeomorphism. A limit of harmonic maps is harmonic, so \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is a harmonic diffeomorphism from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) . Moreover \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to the constant mean curvature hypersurface \( \partial \left( {{F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\right) \) of the area \( a \) in \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) }\right) \) and continue to satisfy the free boundary condition. As a consequence of the standard regularity result of elliptic partial differential equations (see for example [48]), the map \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) and then from (5.3.10) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta .
\]

If \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta \) , we then finish the proof of the claim. So we may assume that \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta \) . We want to show that \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) and the origins \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) . Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are close to isometries, the injectivity radii of the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) at \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) do not go to zero, and we can extract a subsequence which converges to a hyperbolic limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) and the origin \( \widetilde{P} \) and with finite volume. The new limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) has at least as many cusps as the old limit \( \mathcal{H} \) , since we choose \( \mathcal{H} \) with cusps as few as possible. By the definition of convergence, we can find a sequence of compact sets \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) exhausting \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) , and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) such that for each compact set \( \widetilde{B} \) in \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and each integer \( m \)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{ * }\left( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \right)  - {\widetilde{h}}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{m}\left( \widetilde{B}\right) } \rightarrow  0
\]

as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . For large enough \( k \) the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) , and then

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supset  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since the points of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) have a bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Hence we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  : {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Arbitrarily fix \( {\delta }^{\prime } \in  \left( {\delta ,{\delta }_{0}}\right) \) . Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < {\delta }^{\prime }
\]

for all sufficiently large \( k \) . By Lemma 5.3.7, we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) , and then \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) ,{F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) }\right) \) (on compact subsets) is very close to \( \left( {\mathcal{H},{h}_{ij}, P}\right) \) as long as \( \delta \) small enough and \( k \) large enough. Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) is strictly concave and the foliation of a neighborhood of \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) by constant mean curvature hypersurfaces has the area as a function with nonzero gradient, by the implicit function theorem, there exists a unique constant mean curvature hypersurface with the same area \( a \) near \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) in \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for \( t \) close to \( \omega \) . Hence, when \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little. This is a contradiction and we have proved claim (5.3.9).

We further claim that there must be some \( k \) such that \( {\omega }_{k} =  + \infty \) (i.e., we can smoothly continue the family of harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for all \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , in other words, there must be at least one hyperbolic piece persisting). We argue by contradiction. Suppose for each \( k \) large enough, we can continue the family \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  {\omega }_{k} <  + \infty \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Then as before, we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) and origins \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) . For sufficiently large \( k \) , we can obtain diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) which are as close to preserving the metric as we like, where \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) is a sequence of compact sets, exhausting some hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) , of finite volume and with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) ; moreover, the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all the points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) ; and hence

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supseteq  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is at bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) is reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Then we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  : \;{\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, for any \( \widetilde{\delta } > \delta \) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \widetilde{\delta }
\]

for large enough \( k \) . Then a subsequence of \( {G}_{k} \) converges at least in \( {C}^{q - 1}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) topology to a map \( {G}_{\infty } \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . By the same reason as in the argument of previous two paragraphs, the limit map \( {G}_{\infty } \) is a smooth harmonic diffeomorphism from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) , and takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to a constant mean curvature hypersurface \( {G}_{\infty }\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},{\widetilde{h}}_{ij}}\right) \) with the area \( a \) , and also satisfies the free boundary condition. Moreover we still have

(5.3.11)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{\infty }^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Now by Lemma 5.3.7 we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{G}_{\infty }, I}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

By using \( I \) to identify \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}}_{a} \) and \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) , we see that the map \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } \) is a harmonic diffeomorphism of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to itself which satisfies the free boundary condition and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty },{Id}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

From the uniqueness in Lemma 5.3.8 we conclude that \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } = {Id} \) which contradicts with (5.3.11). This shows at least one hyperbolic piece persists. Moreover the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) , for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , is as close to the hyperbolic metric \( {h}_{ij} \) as we like.

We can continue to form other persistent hyperbolic pieces in the same way as long as there are any points \( {P}_{k} \) outside of the chosen pieces where the injectivity radius at times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) are all at least some fixed positive number \( \rho  > 0 \) . The only modification in the proof is to take the new limit \( \mathcal{H} \) to have the least possible number of cusps out of all remaining possible limits.

Note that the volume of the normalized Ricci flow is constant in time. Therefore by combining with Margulis lemma (see for example [55] [76]), we have proved that there exists a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, a small number \( a > 0 \) and a time \( T <  + \infty \) such that for all \( t \) beyond \( T \) we can find diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) of \( {\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{l}\right) }_{a} \) into \( M,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , so that the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close to the hyperbolic metrics as we like and the exceptional part of \( M \) where the points are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) has the injectivity radii everywhere as small as we like.

## Part III: Incompressibility

We remain to show that the boundary tori of any persistent hyperbolic piece are incompressible, in the sense that the fundamental group of the torus injects into that of the whole manifold. The argument of this part is a parabolic version of Schoen and Yau's minimal surface argument in [109, 110, 111].

Let \( B \) be a small positive number and assume the above positive number \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) . Denote by \( {M}_{a} \) a persistent hyperbolic piece of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( a \) with constant mean curvature and denote by \( {M}_{a}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {\overset{ \circ  }{M}}_{a} \) the part of \( M \) exterior to \( {M}_{a} \) . Thus there is a persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \subset  {M}_{a} \) of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( B \) with constant mean curvature. We also denote by \( {M}_{B}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {M}_{B} \) . By Van Kampen’s Theorem, if \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) then it injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) also. Thus we only need to show \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) .

We will argue by contradiction. Let \( T \) be a torus in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) . Suppose \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) does not inject into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) , then by Dehn’s Lemma the kernel is a cyclic subgroup of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) generated by a primitive element. The work of Meeks-Yau [86] or Meeks-Simon-Yau [87] shows that among all disks in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) whose boundary curve lies in \( T \) and generates the kernel, there is a smooth embedded disk normal to the boundary which has the least possible area. Let \( A = A\left( t\right) \) be the area of this disk. This is defined for all \( t \) sufficiently large. We will show that \( A\left( t\right) \) decreases at a rate bounded away from zero which will be a contradiction.

Let us compute the rate at which \( A\left( t\right) \) changes under the Ricci flow. We need to show \( A\left( t\right) \) decrease at least at a certain rate, and since \( A\left( t\right) \) is the minimum area to bound any disk in the given homotopy class, it suffices to find some such disk whose area decreases at least that fast. We choose this disk as follows. Pick the minimal disk at time \( {t}_{0} \) , and extend it smoothly a little past the boundary torus since the minimal disk is normal to the boundary. For times \( t \) a little bigger than \( {t}_{0} \) , the boundary torus may need to move a little to stay constant mean curvature with area \( B \) as the metrics change, but we leave the surface alone and take the bounding disk to be the one cut off from it by the new torus. The change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) of such disk comes from the change in the metric and the change in the boundary.

For the change in the metric, we choose an orthonormal frame \( X, Y, Z \) at a point \( x \) in the disk so that \( X \) and \( Y \) are tangent to the disk while \( Z \) is normal and compute the rate of change of the area element \( {d\sigma } \) on the disk as

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{d\sigma } = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {g}^{ij}\right) }^{T}\left( {\frac{2}{3}r{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }^{T} - 2{\left( {R}_{ij}\right) }^{T}}\right) {d\sigma }
\]

\[
= \left\lbrack  {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right\rbrack  {d\sigma },
\]

since the metric evolves by the normalized Ricci flow. Here \( {\left( \cdot \right) }^{T} \) denotes the tangential projections on the disk. Notice the torus \( T \) may move in time to preserve constant mean curvature and constant area \( B \) . Suppose the boundary of the disk evolves with a normal velocity \( N \) . The change of the area at boundary along a piece of length \( {ds} \) is given by \( {Nds} \) . Thus the total change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{A}}{dt} = \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}.
\]

Note that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + R\left( {X, Z, X, Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {Y, X, Y, X}\right)  + R\left( {Y, Z, Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}R + R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right) .
\]

By the Gauss equation, the Gauss curvature \( K \) of the disk is given by

\[
K = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + \det {II}
\]

where \( {II} \) is the second fundamental form of the disk in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) . This gives at \( t = {t}_{0} \) ,

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } - \iint \left( {K - \det {II}}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}
\]

Since the bounding disk is a minimal surface, we have

\[
\det {II} \leq  0\text{ . }
\]

The Gauss-Bonnet Theorem tells us that for a disk

\[
\int \int {Kd\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} = {2\pi }
\]

where \( k \) is the geodesic curvature of the boundary. Thus we obtain

(5.3.12)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds} - {2\pi }.
\]

Recall that we are assuming \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) increases monotonically to -6 as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . By the evolution equation of the scalar curvature,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  4\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

and then

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {dt} <  + \infty .
\]

This implies that \( r\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) by using the derivatives estimate for the curvatures. Thus for every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we have

\[
\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right)
\]

for \( t \) sufficiently large. And then the first term on RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
\iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) A.
\]

The geodesic curvature \( k \) of the boundary of the minimal disk is the acceleration of a curve moving with unit speed along the intersection of the disk with the torus; since the disk and torus are normal, this is the same as the second fundamental form of the torus in the direction of the curve of intersection. Now if the metric were actually hyperbolic, the second fundamental form of the torus would be exactly 1 in all directions. Note that the persistent hyperbolic pieces are as close to the standard hyperbolic as we like. This makes that the second term of RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{kds} \leq  \left( {1 + {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L
\]

for some sufficiently small positive number \( {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0 \) , where \( L \) is the length of the boundary curve. Also since the metric on the persistent hyperbolic pieces are close to the standard hyperbolic as we like, its change under the normalized Ricci flow is as small as we like; So the motion of the constant mean curvature torus of fixed area \( B \) will have a normal velocity \( N \) as small as we like. This again makes the third term of RHS of (5.3.12) bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{Nds} \leq  {\varepsilon }_{0}L
\]

Combining these estimates, we obtain

(5.3.13)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

on the persistent hyperbolic piece, where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is some sufficiently small positive number.

We next need to bound the length \( L \) in terms of the area \( A \) . Since \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) , for large \( t \) the metric is as close as we like to the standard hyperbolic one; not just on the persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \) but as far beyond as we like. Thus for a long distance into \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) the metric will look nearly like a standard hyperbolic cusplike collar.

Let us first recall a special coordinate system on the standard hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) as follows. The universal cover of the flat torus \( {T}_{1} \) can be mapped conformally to the \( x - y \) plane so that the deck transformation of \( {T}_{1} \) become translations in \( x \) and \( y \) , and so that the Euclidean area of the quotient is 1 ; then these coordinates are unique up to a translation. The hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond the torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) can be parametrized by \( \left\{  {\left( {x, y, z}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \mid  z > 0}\right\} \) with the hyperbolic metric

(5.3.14)

\[
d{s}^{2} = \frac{d{x}^{2} + d{y}^{2} + d{z}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}.
\]

Note that we can make the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish (in the sense that there exists a diffeomorphism from a large neighborhood of the torus \( {T}_{B} \) (of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{B} \) ) on the standard hyperbolic cusp to the above neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) such that the pull-back of the solution metric by the diffeomorphism is as close to the hyperbolic metric as we wish). Then by using this diffeomorphism (up to a slight modification) we can parametrize the cusplike tube of \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) projecting beyond the torus \( T \) in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) by \( \{ \left( {x, y, z}\right)  \mid  z \geq  \zeta \} \) where the height \( \zeta \) is chosen so that the torus in the hyperbolic cusp at height \( \zeta \) has the area \( B \) .

Now consider our minimal disk, and let \( L\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve of the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) in the above coordinate system, and also let \( A\left( z\right) \) be the area of the part of the disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) . We now want to derive a monotonicity formula on the area \( A\left( z\right) \) for the minimal surface.

For almost every \( z \) the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) is a smooth embedded curve or a finite union of them by the standard transversality theorem. If there is more than one curve, at least one of them is not homotopic to a point in \( T \) and represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) such that a part of the original disk beyond height \( z \) continues to a disk that bounds it. We extend this disk back to the initial height \( \zeta \) by dropping the curve straight down. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve we picked at height \( z \) ; of course \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) with equality if it is the only piece. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \) denote the length of the same curve in the \( x - y \) plane dropped down to height \( w \) for \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \) . In the hyperbolic space we would have

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  = \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

exactly. In our case there is a small error proportional to \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and we can also take it proportional to the distance \( z - w \) by which it drops since \( {\left. \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \right| }_{w = z} = \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and the solution metric is close to the hyperbolic in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. Thus, for arbitrarily given \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } > \zeta \) , as the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\left| {\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  - \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) }\right|  \leq  \delta \left( {z - w}\right) \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \) and \( w \) in \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \leq  {\zeta }^{ * } \) . Now given \( \varepsilon \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) pick \( \delta  = {2\varepsilon }/{\zeta }^{ * } \) . Then

(5.3.15)

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  \leq  \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \left\lbrack  {1 + \frac{{2\varepsilon }\left( {z - w}\right) }{w}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

When we drop the curve vertically for the construction of the new disk we get an area \( \widetilde{A}\left( z\right) \) between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) given by

\[
\widetilde{A}\left( z\right)  = \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{\widetilde{L}\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Here and in the following \( o\left( 1\right) \) denotes various small error quantities as the solution metric close to hyperbolic. On the other hand if we do not drop vertically we pick up even more area, so the area \( A\left( z\right) \) of the original disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) has

(5.3.16)

\[
A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Since the original disk minimized among all disks bounded a curve in the primitive generator of the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and the new disk beyond the height \( z \) is part of the original disk, we have

\[
A\left( z\right)  \leq  \widetilde{A}\left( z\right)
\]

and then by combining with (5.3.15),

\[
{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw} \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) z\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{{w}^{2}} + \frac{2\varepsilon z}{{w}^{3}}}\right\rbrack  {dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) L\left( z\right) \frac{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\zeta }\left\lbrack  {1 + \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Here we used the fact that \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) . Since the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\left( {{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right)  = \frac{L\left( z\right) }{z}
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) \frac{\zeta }{z\left( {z - \zeta }\right) }\left\lbrack  {1 - \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\geq  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{z - \zeta } - \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{z}}\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

or equivalently

(5.3.17)

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\log \left\{  {\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right\}   \geq  0.
\]

This is the desired monotonicity formula for the area \( A\left( z\right) \) .

It follows directly from (5.3.16) and (5.3.17) that

\[
\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\zeta }^{2\varepsilon }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

or equivalently

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\left( \frac{z}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon }\frac{z}{z - \zeta }A\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\zeta ,{\zeta }^{ * }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish, we may assume that \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is so large that \( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} > \zeta \) and \( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} - \zeta } \) is close to 1, and also \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is so small that \( {\left( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon } \) is close to 1 . Thus for arbitrarily small \( {\delta }_{0} > 0 \) , we have

(5.3.18)

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) .
\]

Now recall that (5.3.13) states

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }.
\]

We now claim that if

\[
\left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A \geq  0
\]

then \( L = L\left( \zeta \right) \) is uniformly bounded from above.

Indeed by the assumption we have

\[
A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  \frac{\left( 1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

since \( A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  A \) . By combining with (5.3.16) we have some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) satisfying

\[
\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}}\left( {{\zeta }^{ * } - \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}\right)  \leq  {\int }_{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}^{{\zeta }^{ * }}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}{1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L\left( \zeta \right) .
\]

Thus for \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) suitably large, by noting that the solution metric on a large neighborhood of \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

(5.3.19)

\[
L\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{{z}_{0}}{{\zeta }^{ * }}L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

for some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) . It is clear that we may assume the intersection curve between the minimal disk with the torus at this height \( {z}_{0} \) is smooth and embedded. If the intersection curve at the height \( {z}_{0} \) has more than one piece, as before one of them will represent the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and we can ignore the others. Let us move (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) through as small as possible area in the same homotopy class of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) to a curve which is a geodesic circle in the flat torus coming from our special coordinates, and then drop this geodesic circle vertically in the special coordinates to obtain another new disk. We will compare the area of this new disk with the original minimal disk as follows.

Denote by \( G \) the length of the geodesic circle in the standard hyperbolic cusp at height 1 . Then the length of the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) will be \( G/{z}_{0} \) . Observe that given an embedded curve of length \( l \) circling the cylinder \( {S}^{1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) of circumference \( w \) once, it is possible to deform the curve through an area not bigger than \( {lw} \) into a meridian circle. Note that (the piece of) the intersection curve represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) . Note also that the solution metric is sufficiently close to the hyperbolic metric. Then the area of the deformation from (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) to the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{G}{{z}_{0}}\right)  \cdot  L\left( {z}_{0}\right) .
\]

The area to drop the geodesic circle from height \( {z}_{0} \) to height \( \zeta \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{{z}_{0}}\frac{G}{{w}^{2}}{dw}.
\]

Hence comparing the area of the original minimal disk to that of this new disk gives

\[
A\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) G\left\lbrack  {\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}} + \left( {\frac{1}{\zeta } - \frac{1}{{z}_{0}}}\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

By (5.3.18),(5.3.19) and the fact that \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) , this in turn gives

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( {z}_{0}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) G\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{L\left( \zeta \right) }{{\zeta }^{ * }} + \frac{1}{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Since \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is suitably large, we obtain

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  {2G}/\zeta
\]

This gives the desired assertion since \( G \) is fixed from the geometry of the limit hyperbolic manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) and \( \zeta \) is very large as long as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough.

Thus the combination of (5.3.13), (5.3.18) and the assertion implies that either

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq   - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{2G}{\zeta } - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq   - \pi
\]

since the solution metric on a very large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic and \( \zeta \) is very large as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough. This is impossible because \( A \geq  0 \) and the persistent hyperbolic pieces go on forever. The contradiction shows that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) in fact injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) . This proves that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. [

For \( 0 < b \leq  {b}_{\max } \) as above, let \( \mathcal{E}\left( b\right) \) denote the set of all curvature tensors \( S \) for which there exists a tensor \( T \) satisfying the following conditions:

(i) \( T \) satisfies all the algebraic properties of a curvature tensor, except for the first Bianchi identity. Moreover, \( T \geq  0 \) .

(ii) \( S - T \in \) PIC.

(iii) \( \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{11} + \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{22} + \frac{2\gamma }{n}\operatorname{scal}\left( S\right)  \geq  0 \) .

(iv) For every orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) , the following inequality holds:

\[
\operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{22} - \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{11} \leq  {\omega }^{\frac{1}{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left( S\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p = 3}}^{n}\left( {T}_{1p1p} + {T}_{2p2p}\right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
+ 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p = 3}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p1p} + {T}_{2p2p}}\right) .
\]

Moreover, we define \( \mathcal{C}\left( b\right)  = {\ell }_{a, b}\left( {\mathcal{E}\left( b\right) }\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( C{\left( s\right) }_{s \in  \lbrack 0,1)} \subset  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) be a continuous family of closed convex \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) \) -invariant cones of full dimension, such that \( C\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) is contained in the half space of curvature operators with positive scalar curvature. Suppose that for \( \mathrm{R} \in  C\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) the vector field \( X\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  = {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# } \) is contained in the interior of the tangent cone of \( C\left( s\right) \) at \( \mathrm{R} \) for all \( s \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Then for \( \varepsilon ,{h}_{0} > 0 \) there exists a closed convex \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset \( F \subset  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) with the following properties:

(1) \( F \) is invariant under the vector field \( X \) .

(2) \( C\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \subset  F \) .

(3) \( F \smallsetminus  C\left( s\right) \) is relatively compact for all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Let \( F \) denote the minimal closed convex \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) \) - invariant subset which is invariant under the flow of \( X \) and which contains the set

\[
C\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}  .
\]

Notice that \( F \) is the intersection of all subsets which satisfy the above properties. In particular \( F \) is well defined and \( F \subset  C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) . We have to prove that for all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) the set \( F \smallsetminus  C\left( s\right) \) is bounded.

Suppose on the contrary that \( F \smallsetminus  C\left( s\right) \) is not bounded for some \( s \) . Let \( {s}_{0} \geq  \varepsilon \) denote the infimum among all \( s \) with this property. By the choice of \( {s}_{0} \) it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\lambda  \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{1}{\lambda }F \subset  C\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) . We consider the set \( H = H\left( {s}_{0}\right) \) from Lemma 4.2. Notice that the interior of \( {T}_{0}H = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\lambda  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\lambda H} \) contains \( C\left( {s}_{0}\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) . Thus we can find large numbers \( \lambda , r \geq  {h}_{0} \) such that \( F \cap  \{ \mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  = r\} \) is contained in the interior of \( {\lambda H} \) .

We now define \( {F}^{\prime } \) as the union of \( F \cap  \{ \mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  \leq  r\} \) and \( F \cap  \{ \mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\mathrm{R} \geq  r\} \; \cap  {\lambda H} \) . By construction \( {F}^{\prime } \) is convex, invariant under the vector field \( X \) and contains the set \( C\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \mid  \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\} \) . By the definition of \( F \) this implies \( {F}^{\prime } \subset  F \) . By the definition of \( {F}^{\prime } \) we have \( F \subset  {F}^{\prime } \) and equality does not occur - a contradiction.

## 1. Curve-shrinking

Given \( \Gamma \) , the idea for constructing the one-parameter family \( \widetilde{\Gamma }\left( t\right) \) required by Proposition 18.24 is to evolve an appropriate approximation \( \widetilde{\Gamma }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) of \( \Gamma \) by the curve-shrinking flow. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , is a Ricci flow of compact manifolds and that \( c : {S}^{1} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is a family of parameterized, immersed \( {C}^{2} \) -curves. We denote by \( x \) the parameter on the circle. Let \( X\left( {x, t}\right) \) be the tangent vector \( \partial c\left( {x, t}\right) /\partial x \) and let \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  = X\left( {x, t}\right) /\left( {\left| X\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the unit tangent vector to \( c \) . We denote by \( s \) the arc length parameter on \( c \) . We set \( H\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\nabla }_{S\left( {x, t}\right) }S\left( {x, t}\right) \) , the curvature vector of \( c \) with respect to the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . We define the curve-shrinking flow by

\[
\frac{\partial c\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t} = H\left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

where \( c\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a one-parameter family of curves and \( H\left( {x, t}\right) \) is the curvature vector of the curve \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( x \) with respect to the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . We denote by \( k\left( {x, t}\right) \) the curvature function: \( k\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\left| H\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) } \) . We shall often denote the one-parameter family of curves by \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) . Notice that if \( c\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a curve-shrinking flow and if \( x\left( y\right) \) is a reparameterization of the domain circle, then \( {c}^{\prime }\left( {y, t}\right)  = c\left( {x\left( y\right) , t}\right) \) is also a curve-shrinking flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Ricci flow equation is the following evolution equation for a Riemannian metric:

(3.1)

\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right) .
\]

A solution to this equation (or a Ricci flow) is a one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right) \) , parameterized by \( t \) in a non-degenerate interval \( I \) , on a smooth manifold \( M \) satisfying Equation (3.1). If \( I \) has an initial point \( {t}_{0} \) , then \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is called the initial condition of or the initial metric for the Ricci flow (or of the solution).

Proof. Let \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( {\tau , u}\right) \) be a family of curves with \( \gamma \left( {\tau ,0}\right)  = {\gamma }_{Z} \) and with \( \frac{\partial }{\partial u}\gamma \left( {\tau , u}\right)  = \widetilde{Y}\left( {\tau , u}\right) \) . We denote by \( Y \) the horizontal vector field which is the restriction of \( \widetilde{Y} \) to \( {\gamma }_{0} = {\gamma }_{Z} \) . We set \( q\left( u\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma }\left( {\bar{\tau }, u}\right) \) . By restricting to a smaller neighborhood of 0 in the \( u \) -direction, we can assume that \( q\left( u\right)  \in  {\mathcal{U}}_{x}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) for all \( u \) . Then \( \mathcal{L}\left( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{u}\right)  \geq  {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( {q\left( u\right) }\right) \) . Of course, \( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( {q\left( 0\right) }\right)  = \mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{Z}\right) \) . This implies that

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{du}{L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( q\left( u\right) \right) \right| }_{0} = {\left. \frac{d}{du}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{0},
\]

and

\[
{\left. Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \left( \widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) \left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \right) \right| }_{0} = {\left. \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}{L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( q\left( u\right) \right) \right| }_{0} \leq  {\left. \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{0}.
\]

Recall that \( \nabla {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( q\right)  = 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) , so that

\[
{\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( {\bar{\tau }, u}\right) \left| {}_{0}\left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right)  = \left\langle  {\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) {|}_{0},\nabla {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right\rangle   = 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) {|}_{0}, X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right\rangle  .\right|
\]

Thus, by Proposition 6.33, and using the fact that \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = 0 \) , we have

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)  = {\left. Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \left( \widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) \left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \right) \right| }_{0} - {\left. {\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) \right| }_{0}\left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right)  - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) { \mid  }_{0}, X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right\rangle  }^{ * }
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle }\right.
\]

\[
- 4\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  + 2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
\left. {+2{\left| {\nabla }_{X}Y\right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

Equation (6.9) and the fact that \( {\left| Y\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2} = {\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}\frac{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} \) , give

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle  - 4\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left\lbrack  {\frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} - \frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

Using the definition of \( H\left( {X, Y}\right) \) given in Equation (6.12), allows us to write

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left\lbrack  {\sqrt{\tau }\left( {-2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 4{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
+ \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} - \left( {\frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) } + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) \rbrack {d\tau }.
\]

To simplify further, we compute, using Equation (6.9),

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) }\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\right) }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

Consequently, we have

\[
\frac{d\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) }\right) }\right) }{d\tau }
\]

\[
= 2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {\frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) } + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) .
\]

Using this, and the fact that \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = 0 \) , gives

(6.13) \( \operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right) \)

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( {\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right)  - \frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right)  - \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
= \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}} - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right) {d\tau }.
\]

This proves Inequality (6.11). Now we examine when equality holds in this expression. Given an adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) along \( \gamma \) , let \( \mu \left( v\right) \) be a geodesic through \( \gamma \left( {\bar{\tau },0}\right) \) with tangent vector \( Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) . Then there is a one-parameter family \( \mu \left( {\tau , v}\right) \) of minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics with the property that \( \mu \left( {\bar{\tau }, v}\right)  = \mu \left( v\right) \) . Let \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau , v}\right) \) be \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau , v}\right) /\partial v \) . It is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field with \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\bar{\tau },0}\right)  = Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) . Since \( {L}_{x} \circ  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} = \widetilde{L} \) , we see that

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\mu }_{v}\right) {\left| {}_{v = 0} = \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}{L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( \mu \left( u\right) \right) \right| }_{0}.
\]

Hence, the assumption that we have equality in (6.11) implies that

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\mu }_{v}\right) {\left| {}_{v = 0} = \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{u}\right) \right| }_{0}.
\]

Now we extend this one-parameter family to a two-parameter family \( \mu \left( {\tau , u, v}\right) \) so that \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) /\partial v = {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) and \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) /\partial u = Y\left( \tau \right) \) . Let \( w \) be the variable \( u - v \) , and let \( \widetilde{W} \) be the tangent vector in this coordinate direction, so that \( \widetilde{W} = \widetilde{Y} - {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) . We denote by \( W \) the restriction of \( \widetilde{W} \) to \( {\gamma }_{0,0} = {\gamma }_{Z} \) . By Remark 6.15 the second partial derivative of the length of this family in the \( u \) -direction at \( u = v = 0 \) agrees with the second derivative of the length of the original family \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) in the \( u \) -direction.

Claim 6.42.

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = {\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial w}\frac{\partial }{\partial v}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{v = w = 0} = 0.
\]

Proof. Of course, the second cross-partials are equal. By Lemma 6.14 we have

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{v = w = 0} = 2\sqrt{\tau }{\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \langle \widetilde{W}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \rangle  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {\operatorname{Jac}\left( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\right) , W}\right\rangle  {d\tau }.
\]

Since \( W\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = 0 \) and since \( {\nabla }_{{\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }}\left( \widetilde{W}\right)  = {\nabla }_{W}\left( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\right) \) , we see that the boundary term in the above expression vanishes. The integral vanishes since \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

If Inequality (6.11) is an equality, then

\[
{\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = {\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0}.
\]

We write \( \partial /\partial u = \partial /\partial v + \partial /\partial w \) . Expanding the right-hand side and canceling the common terms gives

\[
0 = \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w} + \frac{\partial }{\partial w}\frac{\partial }{\partial v} + \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {w}^{2}}}\right) {\left. \mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0}.
\]

The previous claim tells us that the first two terms on the right-hand side of this equation vanish, and hence we conclude

\[
{\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {w}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = 0.
\]

Since \( W \) vanishes at both endpoints this implies, according to Proposition 6.13, that \( \widetilde{W}\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( \tau \) , or in other words \( Y\left( \tau \right)  = {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) \) for all \( \tau \) . Of course by construction \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field. This shows that equality holds only if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

Conversely, if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field, then inequality between the second variations at the beginning of the proof is an equality. In the rest of the argument we dealt only with equalities. Hence, in this case Inequality (6.11) is an equality.

This shows that we have equality in (6.11) if and only if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

knowledge_statements.title: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_title: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algebraic curvature operator \( R \) is said to be WPIC (weakly positive isotropic curvature) if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) , we have

\[
{R}_{1313} + {R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {R}_{2424} - 2{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.1}
\]

\( R \) is said to be WPIC1 if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.2}
\]

Moreover \( R \) is said to be WPIC2 if for any orthonormal 4-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) .

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {\mu }^{2}{R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.3}
\]

We call \( {C}_{PIC},{C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC2} \) the cones consisting of algebraic curvature operators that satisfy WPIC, WPIC1 or WPIC2 respectively. Moreover, \( R \) is said to be PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 if it’s contained in the interior of \( {C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC1} \) or \( {C}_{PIC2} \) respectively. A manifold \( M \) is a PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 manifold if there exists a metric \( g \) on \( M \) such that its curvature operator is PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 respectively.
