For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perelman’s Differential Harnack Estimate
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Perelman's differential Harnack estimate). Suppose that \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on a closed manifold. Let \( H,\tau  = T - t \) , and \( {v}_{H} \) be as above. Then

(16.82)

\[
{v}_{H} \leq  0,
\]

or, equivalently,

(16.83)

\[
\tau \left( {R + {2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)  + f - n \leq  0.
\]

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof follows the same line of argument as in the previous linear case. Recall from Lemma 6.8 on p. 227 of Part I of this volume the pointwise differential equality:

(16.84)

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta  + R}\right) {v}_{u} =  - {2\tau }{\left| \operatorname{Rc} + \nabla \nabla f - \frac{1}{2\tau }g\right| }^{2}u
\]

for any positive solution \( u \) to the adjoint heat equation. Here \( {v}_{u} \) is defined by (6.20) on p. 227 of Part I of this volume, which is the same as (16.81) with \( H \) replaced by \( u \) . Note that one of the ways in which Perelman obtained his entropy monotonicity formula is essentially by integrating the above equality (see subsection 1.2.2 of Chapter 6 in Part I of this volume).

In §9.3 of [402] Perelman describes the proof of the claim

\[
{v}_{H} \leq  0
\]

by demonstrating in a clever way that for any \( {\tau }_{ * } \) with \( T \geq  {\tau }_{ * } > 0 \) ,

(16.85)

\[
{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}\left( {y,{\tau }_{ * }}\right) h\left( y\right) d{\mu }_{{\tau }_{ * }}\left( y\right)  \leq  0
\]

for any function \( h\left( y\right)  \geq  0 \) with compact support. \( {}^{11} \)

In order to achieve this, in [402] the heat equation

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) h\left( {y, t}\right)  = 0
\]

is solved with the 'initial data'

\[
h\left( {y, T - {\tau }_{ * }}\right)  = h\left( y\right)
\]

\( \left( {t = T - {\tau }_{ * }}\right. \) corresponds to \( \left. {\tau  = {\tau }_{ * }}\right) \) being the given compactly supported nonnegative function. Applying (16.84) to \( u\left( {y,\tau }\right)  = H\left( {y,\tau ;x,0}\right) \) , one derives, via integration by parts, that

(16.86)

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}{hd}{\mu }_{\tau } = {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}h\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } + R}\right) {v}_{H}d{\mu }_{\tau } + {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}\frac{\partial h}{\partial \tau }d{\mu }_{\tau }
\]

\[
=  - 2{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}\tau {\left| \operatorname{Rc} + \nabla \nabla f - \frac{1}{2\tau }g\right| }^{2}{Hhd}{\mu }_{\tau } \leq  0,
\]

---

\( {}^{11} \) Given any \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , we may then take \( h \) limiting to the \( \delta \) -function centered at \( x \) to obtain \( {v}_{H}\left( {x,{\tau }_{ * }}\right)  \leq  0 \) .

---

where we used

\[
{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{h\Delta }{v}_{H}d{\mu }_{\tau } - {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}{\Delta h}\;d{\mu }_{\tau } = 0.
\]

The Li-Yau-type inequality \( {v}_{H} \leq  0 \) , i.e., Theorem 16.44, then follows from the above monotonicity, provided we can establish the following.

Claim.

(16.87)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}{hd}{\mu }_{\tau } \leq  0
\]

The rest of this subsection is devoted to proving the above claim (16.87) following [384]. We shall need the heat kernel parametrix as well as some results on the reduced distance. With respect to the metric \( g\left( \tau \right) \) , let \( {d}_{\tau }\left( {x, y}\right) \) denote the distance function, let \( {B}_{\tau }\left( {x, r}\right) \) denote the ball of radius \( r \) centered at \( x \) , and let \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{\tau } \) denote the volume.

Analogously to Theorem 16.12 we have the following.

THEOREM 16.46 (Ricci flow adjoint heat kernel parametrix). Suppose \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on a closed manifold. Let \( H\left( {y,\tau ;x,0}\right) \) (we also denote this by \( H\left( {x, y,\tau }\right) \) ) be the fundamental solution to the (backward in t) adjoint heat equation (16.80). Then as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) we have

\[
H\left( {y,\tau ;x,0}\right)  \sim  {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-n/2}\exp \left( {-\frac{{d}_{0}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right) }{4\tau }}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 0}}^{\infty }{\tau }^{j}{u}_{j}\left( {x, y,\tau }\right) .
\]

That is, there exist \( \bar{\tau } > 0 \) and a sequence \( {u}_{j} \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {\mathcal{M} \times  \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) such that

\[
H\left( {y,\tau ;x,0}\right)  - {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-n/2}\exp \left( {-\frac{{d}_{0}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right) }{4\tau }}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 0}}^{k}{\tau }^{j}{u}_{j}\left( {x, y,\tau }\right)  = {w}_{k}\left( {x, y,\tau }\right) ,
\]

where

\[
{w}_{k}\left( {x, y,\tau }\right)  = O\left( {\tau }^{k + 1 - \frac{n}{2}}\right)
\]

as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) , uniformly for all \( x, y \in  \mathcal{M} \) . The function \( {u}_{0}\left( {x, y,\tau }\right) \) may be chosen so that \( {u}_{0}\left( {x, x,0}\right)  = 1 \) .

This result was proved by Garofalo and Lanconelli [204] for fundamental solutions of heat-type equations in divergence form. In comparison, for the adjoint heat equation \( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau } - {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) }u + {Ru} = 0 \) there is a zeroth-order term \( {Ru} \) and the Laplacian is with respect to a time-dependent metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . However, one can verify that the argument in [204] carries over to the case of the adjoint heat equation provided \( g\left( t\right) \) is \( {C}^{\infty } \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . We leave this verification as a (somewhat nontrivial) exercise for the reader.

Define the entropy-like quantity

(16.88)

\[
{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right)  \Doteq  {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{v}_{H}{hd}{\mu }_{\tau },
\]

where \( h \) is the previously described solution to the heat equation. It is clear that for any \( \tau \) with \( T \geq  \tau  > 0,{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right) \) is a well-defined quantity. A priori it may blow up as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) .

It turns out that in our course of proving \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right)  \leq  0 \) , we need to show first that there exists \( C > 0 \) , which may depend on the geometry of the Ricci flow solution \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) defined on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) but which is independent of \( \tau \) (as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) ), such that

(16.89)

\[
{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right)  \leq  C
\]

for all \( T \geq  \tau  > 0 \) .

The following lemma supplies the key estimates for this purpose.

LEMMA 16.47 (Gradient estimates for the adjoint heat equation). Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) ,\tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , be a smooth solution to the backward Ricci flow on a closed manifold. Suppose there exist positive constants \( {k}_{1} \) and \( {k}_{2} \) such that on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{R}_{ij}\left( {g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  \geq   - {k}_{1}{g}_{ij}\left( \tau \right) \;\text{ and }\;\max \left\{  {R\left( {y,\tau }\right) ,{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}\left( {y,\tau }\right) }\right\}   \leq  {k}_{2}.
\]

(i) (Gradient estimate for uniformly bounded positive solutions) If \( u \leq \; A \) is a positive solution to the adjoint heat equation on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , then there exist constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} < \infty \) depending only on \( {k}_{1},{k}_{2} \) , and \( n \) such that for \( 0 < \tau  \leq  \min \left\{  {1, T,\frac{1}{2{k}_{2}}}\right\} \) ,

(16.90)

\[
\tau \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}} \leq  \left( {1 + {C}_{1}\tau }\right) \left( {\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  + {C}_{2}\tau }\right) .
\]

(ii) (Gradient estimate for positive solutions) If \( u \) is a positive solution to the adjoint heat equation on \( \mathcal{M} \times  (0, T\rbrack \) , then there exists a constant \( B < \infty \) , depending on the solution \( \{ g\left( \tau \right) {\} }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } \) , such that for

\[
0 < \tau  \leq  \min \left\{  {1, T,\frac{1}{2{k}_{2}}}\right\}  ,
\]

(16.91)

\[
\tau \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}} \leq  \left( {2 + {C}_{1}\tau }\right) \left( {\log \left( {\frac{B}{{\tau }^{n/2}u}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{ud}{\mu }_{\tau }}\right)  + {C}_{2}\tau }\right) .
\]

Here and henceforth we shall use the same notation \( {C}_{i} \) (or \( B \) ) on different lines if the constants differ at most by a multiplicative factor depending only on \( n \) . Note that \( {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{ud}{\mu }_{\tau } \) is independent of \( \tau \) and equals 1 if \( u \) is the fundamental solution. The proof of the lemma given below is a modification of some arguments in Hamilton [249]. See Appendix E of this volume for an exposition of some of the estimates in [249].

Proof. (i) If \( u \) is a solution of \( {\square }^{ * }u = 0 \) , then we compute

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \left( {{g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}u{\nabla }_{j}u}\right)  =  - 4\operatorname{Rc}\left( {\nabla u,\nabla u}\right)  - 2{\left| \nabla \nabla u\right| }^{2} - 2\nabla \left( {Ru}\right)  \cdot  \nabla u,
\]

where we used \( \nabla \left( {{\square }^{ * }u}\right)  \cdot  \nabla u = 0 \) and where the Rc term on the RHS is from both differentiating \( {g}^{ij} \) in time and commuting \( \Delta \) and \( \nabla \) . Hence

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}\right)  = \frac{-4\operatorname{Rc}\left( {\nabla u,\nabla u}\right)  - 2{\left| \nabla \nabla u\right| }^{2} - 2\nabla \left( {Ru}\right)  \cdot  \nabla u}{u}
\]

\[
+ \frac{2\nabla u \cdot  \nabla {\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}} - \frac{2{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{4}}{{u}^{3}} - \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) u
\]

\[
=  - \frac{4\operatorname{Rc}\left( {\nabla u,\nabla u}\right) }{u} - 2\nabla R \cdot  \nabla u - \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}R
\]

\[
- \frac{2}{u}{\left| \nabla \nabla u - \frac{\nabla u \otimes  \nabla u}{u}\right| }^{2}
\]

Applying the assumed bounds for \( \operatorname{Rc}, R \) , and \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \) , we obtain

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}\right)  \leq  \left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1}\frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + 2\left| {\nabla R}\right| \left| {\nabla u}\right|
\]

(16.92)

\[
\leq  \left( {\left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1} + 1}\right) \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + {k}_{2}u
\]

where in the last line we used \( 2\left| {\nabla R}\right| \left| {\nabla u}\right|  \leq  \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + u{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2} \) and \( {\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2} \leq  {k}_{2} \) .

We also compute

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \left( {u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right) \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) u + u\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  + 2\frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}
\]

\[
= \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + {Ru} - {Ru}\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)
\]

(16.93)

\[
\geq  \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} - n{k}_{1}u - {k}_{2}u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right) ,
\]

where we used

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \log u = \frac{\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) u}{u} + \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}} =  - R + \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{{u}^{2}},
\]

\( {\square }^{ * }u = 0, u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  \geq  0 \) , and the upper and lower bounds for \( R \) .

Consider the quantity

\[
\Phi  \Doteq  \varphi \left( \tau \right) \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} - {e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  - {C\tau u},
\]

where below we shall choose \( C \) and the function \( \varphi \left( \tau \right) \) of \( \tau  \geq  0 \) . By combining the above two equations (16.92) and (16.93), we obtain

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \Phi  = \frac{d\varphi }{d\tau }\frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + \varphi \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}
\]

\[
- {k}_{2}{e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  - {e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \left( {u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
- C\left( {u + \tau \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) u}\right)
\]

(16.94)

\[
\leq  \left( {\frac{d\varphi }{d\tau } + \left( {\left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1} + 1}\right) \varphi  - {e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }}\right) \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u}
\]

\[
+ \left( {{k}_{2}\varphi  + n{k}_{1}{e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }}\right) u - C\left( {u - {\tau Ru}}\right) .
\]

Now let \( \varphi \left( \tau \right)  \Doteq  \frac{\tau }{1 + \left( {\left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1} + 1}\right) \tau } \) (note that \( \frac{\tau }{2 + \left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1}} \leq  \varphi \left( \tau \right)  \leq  \tau  \leq  1 \) for \( 0 \leq  \tau  \leq  1) \) . Since in general, for \( c \geq  0 \) ,

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( \frac{\tau }{1 + {c\tau }}\right)  = \frac{1}{{\left( 1 + c\tau \right) }^{2}} \leq  \frac{1}{1 + {c\tau }} = 1 - \frac{c\tau }{1 + {c\tau }},
\]

we have that the function \( \varphi \left( \tau \right) \) satisfies

\[
\frac{d\varphi }{d\tau } + \left( {\left( {4 + n}\right) {k}_{1} + 1}\right) \varphi  - 1 \leq  0.
\]

From this and \( {\tau R} \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) (since \( \left. {\tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2{k}_{2}}}\right) \) , we see that (16.94) implies

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \Phi  \leq  \left( {{k}_{2}\varphi  + n{k}_{1}{e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }}\right) u - \frac{1}{2}{Cu} \leq  0,
\]

provided we choose \( C \doteq  2\left( {{k}_{2} + n{k}_{1}{e}^{{k}_{2}}}\right) \) (since \( \tau ,\varphi  \leq  1 \) ). By the maximum principle, since \( \Phi \left( 0\right)  =  - u\left( 0\right) \log \left( \frac{A}{u\left( 0\right) }\right)  \leq  0 \) , we have

\[
\Phi \left( {x,\tau }\right)  \leq  0
\]

for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( 0 \leq  \tau  \leq  \min \left\{  {1, T,\frac{1}{2{k}_{2}}}\right\} \) . That is, on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \min \left\{  {1, T,\frac{1}{2{k}_{2}}}\right\} \) ,

\[
\varphi \left( \tau \right) \frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} \leq  {e}^{{k}_{2}\tau }u\log \left( \frac{A}{u}\right)  + 2\left( {{k}_{2} + n{k}_{1}{e}^{{k}_{2}}}\right) {\tau u}.
\]

From this one can easily derive (16.90). This completes the proof of part (i) of Lemma 16.47.

(ii) To prove the second part, we first claim that for a positive solution \( u \) to the adjoint heat equation, there exists a constant \( C < \infty \) depending on \( \{ g\left( \tau \right) {\} }_{\tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } \) such that

(16.95)

\[
u\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{C}{{\tau }^{n/2}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}u\left( {z,\tau }\right) d{\mu }_{\tau }\left( z\right)  = \frac{\text{ const }}{{\tau }^{n/2}}.
\]

Assuming (16.95), we have for \( \widetilde{\tau } \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\tau }{2},\tau }\right\rbrack \) that

\[
u\left( {y,\widetilde{\tau }}\right)  \leq  \frac{C}{{\left( \tau /2\right) }^{n/2}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{ud\mu }
\]

since \( {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{ud\mu } \) is constant. Let \( A \Doteq  \frac{C}{{\left( \tau /2\right) }^{n/2}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{ud\mu },\widetilde{u}\left( \widetilde{\tau }\right)  \Doteq  u\left( {\widetilde{\tau } + \frac{\tau }{2}}\right) \) , and \( \widetilde{g}\left( \widetilde{\tau }\right)  \Doteq  g\left( {\widetilde{\tau } + \frac{\tau }{2}}\right) \) . Since \( \widetilde{u} \leq  A \) on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau /2}\right\rbrack \) , we may apply estimate (16.90) using the above quantities to obtain

\[

By the entropy monotonicity formula (16.86) and the mean value theorem we can find \( {\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0}}{\tau }_{k}^{2}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{\left| \operatorname{Rc} + \nabla \nabla f - \frac{1}{2{\tau }_{k}}g\right| }^{2}{Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}} = 0.
\]

---

\( {}^{17} \) The basic idea is that on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) we have

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-n/2}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }}h\left( {y,\tau }\right) {dy} = \frac{n}{2}h\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

The heat kernel parametrix enables the analogue of this formula to carry over to manifolds.

---

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the Hölder inequality we have \( {}^{18} \)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0}}{\tau }_{k}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}\left( {R + {\Delta f} - \frac{n}{2{\tau }_{k}}}\right) {Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}} = 0.
\]

This implies

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}\left( {{\tau }_{k}\left( {R + {2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)  + f - n}\right) {Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}\left( {{\tau }_{k}\left( {{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)  + f - \frac{n}{2}}\right) {Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}}.
\]

Again, integration by parts shows

\[
{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{\tau }_{k}\left( {{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}} = {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{\tau }_{k}\langle \nabla H,\nabla h\rangle d{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}}
\]

\[
=  - {\tau }_{k}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{H\Delta hd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}} \rightarrow  0.
\]

Hence, by (16.113)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}{\mathcal{W}}_{h}\left( {g, H,\tau }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }_{k} \rightarrow  0}}{\int }_{\mathcal{M}}\left( {f - \frac{n}{2}}\right) {Hhd}{\mu }_{{\tau }_{k}} \leq  0.
\]

This proves in (16.114) that we have \( \alpha  \leq  0 \) . The proofs of both (16.87) and Theorem 16.44 are complete.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. G. Perelman [33, Th. 12.1]). Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a compact manifold with positive isotropic curvature of dimension \( n \geq  {12} \) , which does not contain any nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space forms. Let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , denote the solution to the Ricci flow with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . Given a small number \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } > 0 \) and a large number \( {A}_{0} \) , we can find a positive number \( \widehat{r} \) with the following property: If \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time with \( Q \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{A}_{0}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {A}_{0}{Q}^{-1},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

The proof of Theorem 7.2 is an adaptation of Perelman's work [33]. (See also [12], where the four-dimensional case is treated.) By Corollary 1.3, the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature for some function \( f \) satisfying \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{f\left( s\right) }{s} \; = 0 \) and some constant \( \theta  > 0 \) . Let us fix a small number \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , and let \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) denote the constants in Corollary 6.22. It suffices to prove the assertion when \( {A}_{0} \geq  8{C}_{1} \) and \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) . To do that, we argue by contradiction. If the assertion is false, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {j}^{2} \) .

(ii) After dilating by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - {A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack
\]

is not \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

By a point-picking argument, we can arrange that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the following condition:

(iii) If \( \left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right) \) is a point in space-time such that \( \widetilde{t} \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \widetilde{Q} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( \widetilde{t}\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - {A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-1},\widetilde{t}}\right\rbrack \) is, after dilating by the factor \( \widetilde{Q},\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

Our strategy is to rescale the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . We will show that the rescaled flows converge to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. To that end, we proceed in several steps:

Step 1: We first establish a pointwise curvature derivative estimate. By Corollary 6.20, we can find a large constant \( \eta \) , depending only on \( n \) and \( \theta \) , such that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) on every ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Using property (iii) above, we conclude that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( t \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) .

Step 2: We next prove bounds for the higher order covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor. Suppose that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \operatorname{scal} \leq  8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Shi’s interior derivative estimates, we conclude \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we define

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

Here, we allow the possibility that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \infty \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  8 \) for \( 0 < \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta } \) .

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

Clearly, \( {\rho }^{ * } \geq  \frac{1}{100\eta } \) . By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . By Step 2, we obtain bounds for the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, Perelman’s noncollapsing estimate gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we can find a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

For each \( j \) , we can find a unit speed geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( \eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}
\]

if \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) .

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( 8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, it follows from property (iii) and Corollary 6.22 that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty ;
\]

consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  4{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that

\[
8{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s}.
\]

This implies \( 4{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . Moreover, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. Finally, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{q}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in [33, §12.1], there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate established in Step 1, we can extend the metric backwards in time. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now rescale the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 together with Shi's interior derivative estimates, we conclude that the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor are bounded at bounded distance. Combining this with Perelman's noncollapsing estimate, we conclude that (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete smooth limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \; \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Using property (iii) and Corollary 6.22, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Note that the last possibility cannot occur; indeed, if \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a quotient neck, then \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) contains a quotient neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, and Theorem A.1 in [6] then implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption.

We claim that the limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0, contradicting Proposition 6.9. Thus, \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack  }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {2\Lambda }
\]

for each \( A > 1 \) . Hence, if we put \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) , then we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of the Ricci flow that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) . In the next step, we put \( {\tau }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{1} - \frac{1}{{200n}{\Lambda }_{1}} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) , backwards in time to a solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, \( {\Lambda }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{1} \) . Continuing this process, we can extend the solution backwards in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \) id \( \in \) PIC.

Step 6: We claim that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . To prove this, we argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) . Clearly, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) .

By the Harnack inequality (cf. Theorem 6.1 above), the function \( t \mapsto \; \left( {t - {\tau }^{ * }}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right) \) is monotone increasing at each point \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) . Since \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \Lambda \) for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) , we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda
\]

for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using Lemma 8.3(b) in [33], we conclude that

\[
0 \leq   - \frac{d}{dt}{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  C\left( n\right) \sqrt{\frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Integrating over \( t \) gives

\[
{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

By the maximum principle,

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) } \leq  1
\]

for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Hence, we can find a point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}^{\infty } \) such that \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right) \; \leq  4 \) for \( t = {\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda } \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) if \( m \) is sufficiently large. Arguing as in Step 3, we can show that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) \left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } < \infty
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) .

Consequently, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit. If this limit manifold has unbounded curvature, then (by property (iii) above) it contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. Therefore, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit with bounded curvature. Consequently, we can find a constant \( {\Lambda }^{ * } > \Lambda \) (independent of \( A \) ) such that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Using the distance estimate, we obtain \( {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right)  \subset \; {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }}\right) \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Hence, for each \( A > 1 \) , we can find a large integer \( m \) (depending on \( A \) ) such that \( {\tau }_{m} \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{g}\infty \left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {{\tau }_{m}, A}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Using the pointwise derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Since \( {\Lambda }^{ * } \) is independent of \( A \) , we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( t\right)  \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Therefore, the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) , has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) .

To summarize, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence), the rescaled flows converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Here, \( \kappa \) depends only on the initial data. This contradicts statement (ii). This completes the proof of Theorem 7.2.
